note: Grocery-label glossary for tipofthebanana.com. This is not a complete dump of FDA's Substances Added to Food inventory (thousands of mostly obscure flavor chemicals). It prioritizes ingredients, additives, and label terms a US shopper actually sees. Regulatory notes are taken from FDA, USDA, and the eCFR where cited; the inventory itself is a partial list and inclusion is not a use approval. Verdicts appear only on entries FMG has covered and only when a post has a clear editorial angle.

entries.name: Sugar
entries.what: Sucrose from sugar cane or sugar beets, the default sweetener on a grocery label.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is familiar, consistent, and browns. A plant uses it when it wants sweetness plus bulk, and when the label is easier if the word is just "sugar."
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a GRAS nutrient and sweetener. On the Nutrition Facts panel, sugars and added sugars are declared under 21 CFR 101.9.

entries.name: Brown sugar
entries.what: Sucrose with molasses left in or added back, which gives color, moisture, and a mild caramel taste.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Molasses holds water and adds flavor without a separate molasses line when the plant just wants brown-sugar notes in a dough or sauce.

fmg_reveals.title: The brown sugar at the grocery store is usually white sugar with molasses added back
fmg_reveals.finding: The brown sugar at the grocery store is usually white sugar with molasses added back. Light brown is about 3.5% molasses.

entries.name: Turbinado sugar
entries.what: Partially refined cane sugar with some molasses still on the crystals. It is not unprocessed.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can use it for a coarser crystal or a 'less refined' story on the label, with nearly the same sweetness as white sugar.

entries.name: Evaporated cane juice
entries.what: A name some labels still use for cane sugar that was less fully refined. FDA has said the common or usual name is sugar, not juice.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It can sound closer to a juice than to sugar. FDA's guidance is that 'evaporated cane juice' is not the common or usual name and can be misleading.
entries.regulatory_note: FDA's 2016 guidance says evaporated cane juice should not be used as the common or usual name; the ingredient is sugar.

entries.name: Dextrose
entries.what: A simple sugar, usually from corn starch in the US, that is a little less sweet than table sugar and dissolves fast.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It browns, it ferments cleanly, it carries flavor, and it can be dosed precisely in dry mixes, cured meats, and baking.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1857 (dextrose).

fmg_reveals.title: MSG is made by feeding sugar to a soil bacterium

entries.name: Fructose
entries.what: A simple sugar sweeter than sucrose, sold as a crystalline powder or as part of syrups and fruit-juice concentrates.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Because it is sweeter than sugar, a plant can use less of it by weight for the same sweetness, or use it in products that need a very soluble sweetener.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1866 for high fructose corn syrup; crystalline fructose is also used under GRAS conditions. Added sugars rules in 21 CFR 101.9 still apply.

entries.name: Invert sugar
entries.what: Sucrose that has been split into glucose and fructose, usually as a syrup that stays smooth and resists crystallizing.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Candy, fondant, and icings need a syrup that will not grain out. Invert sugar holds moisture and stays glossy.

entries.name: Corn syrup
entries.what: A starch-based syrup (usually corn in the US) that is mildly sweet, thick, and helps keep sugar from crystallizing. Dried, it is sold as corn syrup solids.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is cheaper than sugar on a solids basis in many formulas, it adds body, and it keeps confectionery and sauces smooth. Corn syrup solids do the same job in a dry or 'no cream' formula.
entries.regulatory_note: Corn syrup is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1865. Nutrition labeling of sugars and added sugars is under 21 CFR 101.9.

entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1866. It counts toward added sugars on the Nutrition Facts label under 21 CFR 101.9.

entries.name: Maltodextrin
entries.what: Starch, usually from corn, that has been broken down into a bland, slightly sweet powder. It is a carbohydrate. In the US it is not listed on the 'sugars' line.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It bulks out a mix, carries flavor, thickens a little, and dissolves cleanly. It can be a first ingredient after water and still leave the 'sugars' line looking smaller than the carbohydrate line.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1444, with a dextrose equivalent (DE) of less than 20.

entries.name: Honey
entries.what: A plant-made sweetener produced by honey bees, mostly fructose and glucose, with water and trace flavors from the nectar.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It sweetens, holds moisture, and supports a 'made with honey' claim. A formula can still be mostly other sugars, with honey used for flavor and the claim.

entries.name: Maple syrup
entries.what: Boiled sap of maple trees. Imitation 'pancake syrup' is usually corn syrup with maple flavor and is a different product.
entries.why_plants_use_it: The real syrup is used when the plant wants the flavor and the name. A cheaper 'syrup' uses corn syrup and flavor instead.

entries.name: Molasses
entries.what: The dark syrup left when sugar is crystallized from cane or beet juice. It is less sweet than sugar and brings color and a strong flavor.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A little goes a long way for color and flavor in sauces, baked beans, bread, and brown sugar. It also holds moisture.

entries.name: Agave nectar
entries.what: A syrup from agave inulin that has been hydrolyzed into a fructose-rich liquid, often sweeter than sugar.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It dissolves easily and is often used in beverages and 'natural' sweetener lines. It still counts as an added sugar.

entries.name: Fruit juice concentrate
entries.what: Fruit juice with most of the water removed. On a label it can sweeten a product that wants to avoid the word 'sugar.'
entries.why_plants_use_it: It lets a plant sweeten with something that still sounds like fruit. For 'no added sugar' claims, 21 CFR 101.60 treats concentrated fruit juice used to sweeten as an added-sugar ingredient.
entries.regulatory_note: Under 21 CFR 101.60(c)(2), a 'no added sugar' claim is not allowed if the product contains an ingredient containing added sugars such as concentrated fruit juice used for sweetening.

entries.name: Date paste
entries.what: Cooked-down or dried dates, used as a paste, syrup, or powder to sweeten bars and baked goods.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It can replace a named sugar on a 'sweetened with dates' label while still doing the job of a caloric sweetener and binder.

entries.name: Brown rice syrup
entries.what: A syrup made by breaking down rice starch into glucose, maltose, and oligosaccharides. It is less sweet than sugar.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It binds granola and cereal bars and supports a grain-based sweetener story. It still contributes carbohydrate and sugars.

fmg_reveals.title: Frosted Mini-Wheats aren't vegetarian
fmg_reveals.finding: Frosted Mini-Wheats aren't vegetarian. The ingredients are whole grain wheat and sugar, then 2% or less of brown rice syrup and gelatin, plus iron and folic acid.

entries.name: Barley malt syrup
entries.what: A syrup or extract from sprouted barley, with a malt flavor and moderate sweetness.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is used for flavor and color in cereals, bagels, beers, and malted milks, not only for sweetness.

entries.name: Coconut sugar
entries.what: Sugar crystallized from the sap of coconut palm blossoms. Chemically it is still mostly sucrose.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It offers a brown-sugar flavor and a different origin story, with similar bulk and browning to regular sugar.

entries.name: Tapioca syrup
entries.what: A starch syrup from cassava (tapioca), used like corn syrup as a binder and mild sweetener.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is useful when a plant wants a corn-free syrup in bars, gummies, or 'clean' confectionery.

entries.name: Erythritol
entries.what: A sugar alcohol (polyol) with almost no calories in FDA's labeling guidance, used to bulk and sweeten 'sugar free' and keto products.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It provides bulk that high-intensity sweeteners lack, with a sugar-like crystal. Plants use it in tabletop blends, beverages, and 'keto' baked goods.
entries.regulatory_note: Erythritol is used under GRAS notices. FDA has issued guidance on its caloric declaration. Polyols may require a laxation warning if present at significant levels (21 CFR 101.17(i) for some polyols).

entries.name: Sorbitol
entries.what: A sugar alcohol used as a sweetener, humectant, and bulking agent, especially in sugar-free candy and toothpaste-like gels.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It holds moisture so a product stays chewy, and it sweetens without sucrose. Too much can have a laxative effect, which is why some labels carry a notice.
entries.regulatory_note: Used in food; 21 CFR 101.80 addresses health claims for sugar alcohols and dental caries. 21 CFR 101.17(i) requires a laxation warning when a food can reasonably be expected to be consumed in amounts that may cause a laxative effect, for specified polyols including sorbitol.

entries.name: Xylitol
entries.what: A sugar alcohol about as sweet as sucrose, often used in sugar-free gum and mints.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It sweetens, does not feed the same oral bacteria as sugar in the way sucrose does, and supports certain dental claims when the rules in 21 CFR 101.80 are met.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a nutritive sweetener and humectant at 21 CFR 172.395. 21 CFR 101.80 addresses dental-caries health claims for sugar alcohols.

entries.name: Maltitol
entries.what: A sugar alcohol used to replace sugar in chocolate, candy, and baked 'sugar free' products because it is close to sugar in bulk and sweetness.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It lets a plant make a sugar-free chocolate or cookie that still has weight and snap. It can still cause GI discomfort at higher intakes.

entries.name: Mannitol
entries.what: A sugar alcohol used as a sweetener, anti-caking agent, and dusting powder on chewing gum and 'sugar free' confections.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It does not pick up moisture as readily as some other polyols, so it is useful as a dusting sugar that stays dry.
entries.regulatory_note: Mannitol is an interim food additive at 21 CFR 180.25, with labeling provisions including a notice about laxative effects when used at certain levels.

entries.name: Isomalt
entries.what: A sugar alcohol made from sucrose, used in hard candies and decorations because it holds shape and does not brown like sugar.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is stable in cooked hard candy and decorative work, and it is less hygroscopic than sucrose in those uses.

entries.name: Lactitol
entries.what: A sugar alcohol made from lactose, used as a bulk sweetener in sugar-free chocolate and baked goods.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It provides the weight and some of the texture of sugar with fewer calories, often blended with a high-intensity sweetener.

entries.name: Hydrogenated starch hydrolysates
entries.what: A family of polyol syrups made by hydrogenating broken-down starch. They act like a sugar-free corn syrup.
entries.why_plants_use_it: They give body and chew to sugar-free candy and bars without crystallizing the way sugar can.

entries.name: Aspartame
entries.what: A high-intensity sweetener made from two amino acids, many times sweeter than sugar, used in diet sodas, gums, and tabletop packets.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A tiny amount replaces a lot of sugar in a beverage or tabletop packet, so the formula can be low-calorie. It is not heat-stable in all cooking uses, so plants often pick something else for baked goods.
entries.regulatory_note: Approved as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.804. Products with aspartame must bear a statement that they contain phenylalanine.

entries.name: Sucralose
entries.what: A high-intensity sweetener made from sugar that has been chemically modified so it is very sweet and largely not metabolized as sugar.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is heat-stable compared with aspartame, so a plant can use it in beverages, baked mixes, and 'sugar free' syrups.
entries.regulatory_note: Approved as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.831. FDA's inventory lists it as a nutritive sweetener in the technical-effect field; it is used as a high-intensity sweetener.

fmg_reveals.title: The citric acid in a Celsius is grown by a mold, and the taurine was never near a bull
fmg_reveals.finding: The citric acid in a Celsius is grown by a mold, and the taurine was never near a bull. The list is carbonated water, citric acid, taurine, vegetable juice for color, guarana seed extract, green tea extract, caffeine, ascorbic acid, sucralose, glucuronolactone, ginger root extract and a vitamin pack.

entries.name: Acesulfame potassium
entries.what: A high-intensity sweetener, often blended with sucralose or aspartame because the blend tastes closer to sugar than either one alone.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is heat-stable and cheap at use levels. Blending masks a bitter or lingering note that some high-intensity sweeteners have on their own.
entries.regulatory_note: Approved as a non-nutritive sweetener at 21 CFR 172.800.

entries.name: Saccharin
entries.what: A high-intensity sweetener, one of the oldest still on the US market, used in some tabletop packets and diet products.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is very sweet at low cost and is heat-stable. It is often blended to round off a bitter aftertaste.
entries.regulatory_note: Saccharin and its salts are listed as interim food additives at 21 CFR 180.37, with conditions of use and labeling requirements.

entries.name: Neotame
entries.what: A high-intensity sweetener related to aspartame, used at very low levels in some beverages and tabletop products.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is much sweeter than aspartame, so a plant uses even less of it. It is more heat-stable than aspartame in some uses.
entries.regulatory_note: Approved as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.829.

entries.name: Advantame
entries.what: A high-intensity sweetener related to aspartame, used at extremely low levels.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A very small amount is enough, which helps in beverages and reduced-sugar formulas where other ingredients already take up space.
entries.regulatory_note: Approved as a non-nutritive sweetener at 21 CFR 172.803.

entries.name: Stevia leaf extract
entries.what: High-intensity sweeteners purified from stevia leaves, or made to match those glycosides. The sweet compounds are steviol glycosides, not the whole leaf.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can sweeten a 'no artificial sweeteners' product with a leaf-derived or fermentation-made glycoside. The extract is many times sweeter than sugar, so it is used in tiny amounts, often with a bulking agent.
entries.regulatory_note: Certain high-purity steviol glycosides are used in food under FDA GRAS notices. The whole leaf and crude extracts are not approved as sweeteners. There is no single food-additive listing in 21 CFR Part 172 for all stevia preparations.

entries.name: Monk fruit extract
entries.what: A high-intensity sweetener from monk fruit (luo han guo). The sweet compounds are mogrosides, usually sold as a concentrated extract, often blended with erythritol.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It supports a 'no artificial sweeteners' or keto claim. The extract is so sweet it is almost always cut with a bulk sweetener so a plant can scoop or dissolve it.
entries.regulatory_note: Luo han fruit concentrate appears in FDA's Substances Added to Food inventory as a flavoring agent. Monk fruit extracts are also the subject of FDA GRAS notices for sweetener use.

entries.name: Allulose
entries.what: A low-calorie sugar (a rare sugar) that tastes close to sucrose and browns like sugar, used in 'reduced sugar' ice creams, bars, and syrups.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It gives some of sugar's browning and mouthfeel with fewer calories than sucrose. A plant uses it when a high-intensity sweetener alone would taste thin.
entries.regulatory_note: Allulose is used under GRAS notices. FDA's 2020 guidance says allulose need not be included in 'Total Sugars' or 'Added Sugars' on the Nutrition Facts label, and may be declared at 0.4 kcal/g.

entries.name: Thaumatin
entries.what: A sweet-tasting protein from the katemfe fruit, used more often as a flavor modifier than as the main sweetener.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A very small amount can round off bitterness or lift sweetness in a high-intensity blend, which is useful in beverages and oral-care-adjacent foods.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed in FDA's Substances Added to Food inventory as a flavoring agent or adjuvant.

entries.name: FD&C Blue No. 1
entries.what: A certified synthetic blue dye, often listed as Blue 1. It is one of the FD&C colors still used in US cereals, drinks, and candy.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses a certified dye when it wants a bright, consistent shade that survives processing and shelf life, at a very low use level.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed for food use at 21 CFR 74.101. It is subject to FDA batch certification. See FDA's summary of color additives for food. Always check the listing regulation for uses and restrictions.

fmg_reveals.finding: Cap'N Crunch Berries have no berries in them. The ingredient list is corn flour, sugar, oat flour, palm or coconut oil, salt and molasses, then Red 40, Yellow 5, Blue 1, Yellow 6 and natural and artificial flavor.

entries.name: FD&C Blue No. 2
entries.what: A certified synthetic blue dye, listed as Blue 2, used for some blues and for blending toward purple or brown shades.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses a certified dye when it wants a bright, consistent shade that survives processing and shelf life, at a very low use level.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed for food use at 21 CFR 74.102. It is subject to FDA batch certification. See FDA's summary of color additives for food. Always check the listing regulation for uses and restrictions.

entries.name: FD&C Green No. 3
entries.what: A certified synthetic green dye, listed as Green 3. It is used less often than the reds and yellows on grocery shelves.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses a certified dye when it wants a bright, consistent shade that survives processing and shelf life, at a very low use level.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed for food use at 21 CFR 74.203. It is subject to FDA batch certification. See FDA's summary of color additives for food. Always check the listing regulation for uses and restrictions.

entries.name: Orange B
entries.what: A certified synthetic color with a narrow permitted use: only in the casings of frankfurters and sausages, not as a general food dye.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It was listed for coloring sausage casings so the surface looks a consistent orange-red. You should not see it as a general ingredient in other foods.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed at 21 CFR 74.250 with a restricted use: only for coloring the casings of frankfurters and sausages, with a maximum level stated in the regulation.

entries.name: Citrus Red No. 2

fmg_reveals.title: The cheese sauce in Kraft Macaroni & Cheese doesn't list cheese
fmg_reveals.finding: The cheese sauce in Kraft Macaroni & Cheese doesn't list cheese. The blue box packet is whey, milkfat, salt, milk protein concentrate and sodium triphosphate, then under 2% of starch, acids, paprika, turmeric and annatto for color, enzymes and cheese culture.

fmg_reveals.title: Kraft removed the artificial dyes from Mac & Cheese in Dec 2015 but didn't tell anyone until March
fmg_reveals.finding: Kraft removed the artificial dyes from Mac & Cheese in Dec 2015 but didn't tell anyone until March. They swapped Yellow 5 and 6 for paprika, annatto and turmeric and kept shipping the same blue box with a new ingredient list.

entries.name: Turmeric oleoresin
entries.what: A concentrated extract of turmeric, used for yellow color without the bulk or full flavor of the ground spice.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses an exempt color when it wants a shade from a plant, mineral, or other listed source, or when it wants to avoid a certified dye on the label.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed for food use at 21 CFR 73.615. It is exempt from FDA batch certification. See FDA's summary of color additives for food. Always check the listing regulation for uses and restrictions.

entries.name: Sodium benzoate
entries.what: A salt of benzoic acid used to slow the growth of yeasts and molds, especially in acidic foods and drinks.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is inexpensive and effective in products that are already tart — sodas, pickles, sauces, and dressings — so a plant can keep a long shelf life without raising the heat treatment.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1733, with use in accordance with good manufacturing practice, and as a prior-sanctioned chemical preservative at 21 CFR 181.23.

fmg_reveals.title: The soy sauce packet in your takeout bag isn't soy sauce
fmg_reveals.finding: The soy sauce packet in your takeout bag isn't soy sauce. The biggest maker, Kari-Out in New Jersey, lists water, salt, hydrolyzed soy and corn protein, caramel color and sodium benzoate.

entries.name: Potassium sorbate
entries.what: A salt of sorbic acid used to slow yeasts and molds in cheeses, dried fruit, baked goods, drinks, and many 'refrigerate after opening' products.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It lets a plant keep a product stable after it is opened, or cut the mold risk on a high-moisture food, without a harsher heat process.
entries.regulatory_note: Potassium sorbate is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 182.3640. Sorbic acid is listed at 21 CFR 182.3089.

entries.name: Calcium propionate
entries.what: A salt of propionic acid used to keep bread and other baked goods from going moldy.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A packaged loaf has to last days on a shelf or in a bag. Propionates slow mold without changing the bread's flavor much at typical use levels.
entries.regulatory_note: Calcium propionate is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 182.3221; sodium propionate at 21 CFR 182.3784.

entries.name: Sodium nitrite
entries.what: A curing salt used in bacon, ham, hot dogs, and jerky. It fixes a pink color, adds a cured flavor, and limits the growth of certain bacteria, including Clostridium botulinum, in cured meats.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant that wants a stable cured meat uses nitrite because it does several jobs at once: color, flavor, and safety in an anaerobic, shelf-stable or vacuum-packed product. 'Uncured' and 'no added nitrites' products often use celery powder or cultured celery instead, which still supplies nitrate/nitrite.
entries.regulatory_note: Use in meat and poultry is regulated by USDA FSIS (9 CFR), not only FDA. Sodium nitrite is a permitted curing agent, with maximum ingoing levels set in FSIS regulations and guidance. FDA also has food-additive listings for certain uses.

fmg_reveals.finding: The bag says no added nitrites. The same bag in Britain says sodium nitrite.

fmg_reveals.finding: Jack Link's beef jerky says no added nitrites on the bag. The asterisk under it says except those from cultured celery extract.

entries.name: Sodium nitrate
entries.what: A curing salt that can convert to nitrite in the product. It is used in some longer-cured meats.
entries.why_plants_use_it: In a slow cure, nitrate provides a reservoir that becomes nitrite over time, which is useful in dry-cured products that sit for weeks.
entries.regulatory_note: Use in meat and poultry is regulated by USDA FSIS, with permitted uses and limits in 9 CFR and FSIS guidance.

fmg_reveals.title: Your uncured bacon is cured
fmg_reveals.finding: Your uncured bacon is cured. Pick up a pack and find the line that says no nitrates or nitrites added except those naturally occurring in celery powder.

entries.name: Cultured celery extract
entries.what: Celery that is high in nitrate, often cultured so the nitrate is converted toward nitrite, then dried and added to meat. It is used to cure a product that still says 'no added nitrites' or 'uncured.'
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can get a cured color and a cured-meat safety function without putting 'sodium nitrite' on the ingredient list. FSIS still requires a qualifying statement such as 'except those naturally occurring in celery powder' when that claim is made.
entries.regulatory_note: FSIS treats these as sources of nitrate/nitrite. Products labeled 'uncured' or 'no nitrates or nitrites added' that use celery powder must include a qualifying statement (for example, 'except those naturally occurring in …') under FSIS labeling rules.

fmg_reveals.finding: The bag says no added nitrites. The same bag in Britain says sodium nitrite.

fmg_reveals.title: Jack Link's beef jerky says no added nitrites on the bag
fmg_reveals.finding: Jack Link's beef jerky says no added nitrites on the bag. The asterisk under it says except those from cultured celery extract.

fmg_reveals.title: Your uncured bacon is cured
fmg_reveals.finding: Your uncured bacon is cured. Pick up a pack and find the line that says no nitrates or nitrites added except those naturally occurring in celery powder.

entries.name: Sodium erythorbate
entries.what: An isomer of vitamin C used in cured meats as a cure accelerator and antioxidant. It helps the nitrite do its color job faster and more evenly.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It shortens the curing reaction and helps keep the pink color, which matters on a high-speed bacon or hot-dog line.

entries.name: BHA
entries.what: A synthetic antioxidant used to keep fats and oils from going rancid, often in packaging, cereals, chewing gum, and fried snacks.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A small amount protects a fat-containing product through a long warehouse life, especially when the fat would otherwise oxidize.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.110, with uses and limits, and in other sections for related uses.

entries.name: BHT
entries.what: A synthetic antioxidant, often used with BHA, to slow rancidity in fats, cereals, and packaged foods.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Same job as BHA: keep a fat-containing product from tasting stale before the sell-by date.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.115, with uses and limits.

entries.name: TBHQ
entries.what: A synthetic antioxidant used especially in refined vegetable oils and fried foods to delay rancidity.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is effective in the oils used to fry snacks and instant noodles, so the oil and the finished food last longer in the bag.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.185, with a maximum total antioxidant limit when used alone or with BHA, BHT, or propyl gallate.

fmg_reveals.title: Top Ramen noodles are fried before they go in the bag
fmg_reveals.finding: Top Ramen noodles are fried before they go in the bag. The list starts with enriched flour and palm oil, then salt, and TBHQ is near the end.

entries.name: Propyl gallate
entries.what: A synthetic antioxidant used in fats and oils, often in combination with BHA or BHT.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Blends of antioxidants can cover a wider range of fats and process conditions than one antioxidant alone.
entries.regulatory_note: Used under food-additive listings, including 21 CFR 172.615 (chewing gum) and other listed uses; also used in fats within prescribed limits.

entries.name: Mixed tocopherols
entries.what: Vitamin E compounds used as antioxidants in fats, cereals, and 'natural flavor' systems, rather than only as a nutrient.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can slow rancidity and list a vitamin-related name instead of BHA, BHT, or TBHQ.
entries.regulatory_note: Tocopherols are listed as GRAS, including 21 CFR 182.3890 and 184.1890, for use as inhibitors of oxidation or as nutrients, depending on the listing.

entries.name: Rosemary extract
entries.what: A concentrated extract of rosemary used as an antioxidant in fats, meat, and snacks. The working compounds are mostly phenolic antioxidants from the herb.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It lets a plant delay rancidity and still put a kitchen-herb name on the ingredient list instead of TBHQ or BHA.
entries.regulatory_note: Rosemary, rosemary oil, and rosemary oleoresin are listed among GRAS flavoring substances at 21 CFR 182.10 and 182.20. Antioxidant use of rosemary extract is also the subject of GRAS notices.

entries.name: Calcium disodium EDTA
entries.what: A chelating agent that binds metals so they cannot catalyze color or flavor changes, used in mayonnaise, canned beans, and some sauces and dressings.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Trace iron or copper can turn a dressing gray or rancid. EDTA ties those metals up so the product stays the same color and flavor for longer.
entries.regulatory_note: Calcium disodium EDTA is listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.120, with specific permitted foods and limits. Disodium EDTA is listed at 21 CFR 172.135.

fmg_reveals.title: Duke's mayonnaise has no sugar in it, and Hellmann's and Kraft both do
fmg_reveals.finding: Duke's mayonnaise has no sugar in it, and Hellmann's and Kraft both do. Duke's lists soybean oil, eggs, water, distilled and cider vinegar, salt, oleoresin paprika, natural flavors and calcium disodium EDTA.

entries.name: Natamycin
entries.what: An antifungal used on the surface of some cheeses to slow mold.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A shredded or block cheese that has to travel and sit in a case is vulnerable to surface mold. Natamycin is applied as a surface treatment rather than as a bulk preservative.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.155 for use on specified cheeses, with a maximum residual level.

fmg_reveals.title: The Philadelphia in the tub isn't cream cheese
fmg_reveals.finding: Cream cheese has a federal standard: at least 33% milkfat, no more than 55% moisture. Cream cheese spread has none.

entries.name: Nisin
entries.what: A bacteriocin (an antimicrobial peptide) produced by Lactococcus lactis, used in some cheeses and heat-processed foods to slow certain gram-positive spoilage and spore-forming bacteria.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It can add a margin of safety or shelf life in a product where a plant does not want to raise salt, acid, or heat any further.
entries.regulatory_note: Nisin preparation is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1538, with conditions of use.

entries.name: Sulfur dioxide
entries.what: Sulfur dioxide and sulfite salts used to prevent browning and to slow microbes in dried fruit, wine, some potatoes, and other foods.
entries.why_plants_use_it: They keep dried fruit looking bright and help control spoilage in wine and some processed potatoes. They are also a labeled allergen-class substance for sensitive people.
entries.regulatory_note: Several sulfites are listed as GRAS (for example sulfur dioxide at 21 CFR 182.3862, sodium metabisulfite at 182.3766) with use limitations. They are not to be used on foods that are recognized as a source of vitamin B1, and 21 CFR 101.100 / 130.9 and related labeling rules require sulfite declaration when present at 10 ppm or more.

fmg_reveals.title: Unless they're organic, your grapes were fumigated with sulfur dioxide after picking
fmg_reveals.finding: Unless they're organic, your grapes were fumigated with sulfur dioxide after picking. California grows 99% of US table grapes and the standard practice is to gas them right after packing, then about once a week in cold storage.

entries.name: Cultured dextrose
entries.what: Dextrose (or sugar) that has been fermented by food-grade cultures, then dried. The fermentate contains organic acids and other metabolites that slow spoilage.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can extend shelf life in a deli salad, sauce, or baked product and list something that sounds like a cultured dairy-adjacent ingredient rather than a classic preservative name.
entries.regulatory_note: Cultured dextrose preparations are used under GRAS notices; they may not appear under that common name as a single line in the Substances Added to Food inventory.

entries.name: Vinegar powder
entries.what: Vinegar that has been dried onto a carrier so it can be added as a powder. The working acid is still acetic acid.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It lowers pH and slows spoilage in a dry mix or a seasoned meat, and the ingredient name stays 'vinegar' instead of 'acetic acid' or a benzoate.

entries.name: Sodium diacetate
entries.what: A salt related to vinegar (acetic acid) used to flavor and to slow certain microbes in breads, snacks, and seasonings.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It gives a salt-and-vinegar bite and a bit of preservation in a dry seasoning or a baked product.
entries.regulatory_note: Sodium acetate is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1721; sodium diacetate at 21 CFR 184.1754.

entries.name: Sodium lactate
entries.what: A salt of lactic acid used in meat and poultry to hold moisture and to slow certain bacteria, often alongside sodium diacetate.
entries.why_plants_use_it: In a cooked sausage or deli meat, it helps shelf life and yield without a large change in flavor at typical use levels.

entries.name: Dimethyl dicarbonate
entries.what: A processing aid used to sterilize cold-filled drinks (often wine, juice, and some teas). It breaks down quickly and is not meant to remain as such in the finished drink.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can reduce yeasts in a beverage without a long heat process that would dull the flavor.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.133, with permitted beverages, maximum use levels, and the requirement that it decomposes; dimethyl carbonate is a breakdown product.

entries.name: Benzoic acid
entries.what: The acid form of the benzoate preservatives, used in some acidic foods and as the parent compound of sodium benzoate.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Same job as sodium benzoate: control yeast and mold in a tart product.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1021, and as a prior-sanctioned chemical preservative at 21 CFR 181.23.

entries.name: Lecithin
entries.what: A mixture of phospholipids, usually from soy, sunflower, or egg, used to blend oil and water and to keep chocolate and baked goods from separating or blooming.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A little lecithin lets a plant mix fat into a coating, a spray, a candy, or a dough and keep it stable. Sunflower lecithin is often used when a plant wants to avoid soy on the label.
entries.regulatory_note: Lecithin is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1400.

fmg_reveals.title: The Texas Roadhouse honey cinnamon butter at the grocery store has no butter in it
fmg_reveals.finding: The Texas Roadhouse honey cinnamon butter at the grocery store has no butter in it. The tub reads soybean oil, water, honey, palm oil, palm kernel oil, salt, cinnamon, soy lecithin, monoglycerides, pea protein, preservatives, natural flavors and beta carotene for color.

fmg_reveals.title: Your strawberry Twizzlers have no licorice in them
fmg_reveals.finding: Your strawberry Twizzlers have no licorice in them. The list is corn syrup, wheat flour, sugar and cornstarch, then palm oil, salt, artificial flavor, citric acid, mineral oil, Red 40 and soy lecithin at 2% or less.

fmg_reveals.title: A can of PAM olive oil spray says 0 calories and 0 grams of fat
fmg_reveals.finding: A can of PAM olive oil spray says 0 calories and 0 grams of fat. The ingredients are extra virgin olive oil, soy lecithin and dimethyl silicone.

entries.name: Mono- and diglycerides
entries.what: Emulsifiers made by splitting fat and re-attaching one or two fatty acids to glycerol. They are among the most common emulsifiers in bread, ice cream, peanut butter, and 'buttery' spreads. Apeel-type produce coatings use the same family.
entries.why_plants_use_it: They help bread stay soft, keep ice cream smooth, and keep oil and water from separating in a spread. They can also be used as an invisible coating on fresh produce; in that use, stores may not have to list them on a sticker.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1505. Related esters have their own listings.

fmg_reveals.title: The Texas Roadhouse honey cinnamon butter at the grocery store has no butter in it
fmg_reveals.finding: The Texas Roadhouse honey cinnamon butter at the grocery store has no butter in it. The tub reads soybean oil, water, honey, palm oil, palm kernel oil, salt, cinnamon, soy lecithin, monoglycerides, pea protein, preservatives, natural flavors and beta carotene for color.

fmg_reveals.title: Your apple can be coated with Apeel and the store doesn't have to tell you
fmg_reveals.finding: Your apple can be coated with Apeel and the store doesn't have to tell you. It's mono and diglycerides, the same emulsifier that's in bread, made from plant oil, and you can't see it or taste it.

fmg_reveals.title: Land O Lakes Fat Free Half & Half is mostly skim milk and corn syrup
fmg_reveals.finding: Land O Lakes Fat Free Half & Half is mostly skim milk and corn syrup. The carton lists skim milk, corn syrup and cream, then 0.5% or less of carrageenan, sodium citrate, dipotassium phosphate, mono and diglycerides, vitamin A palmitate and color added.

entries.name: DATEM
aliases: diacetyl tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
mono- and diglycerides, diacetyltartaric acid esters
entries.what: An emulsifier made by reacting mono- and diglycerides with tartaric and acetic acid groups. It is a workhorse in commercial bread.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It strengthens dough so a high-speed bakery can get more volume and a finer crumb with less risk of the loaf collapsing.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1101.

entries.name: Sodium stearoyl lactylate
entries.what: An emulsifier and dough strengthener used in bread, buns, and some fillings and creamers.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It helps dough hold gas and stay soft, and it can keep a filling or a non-dairy creamer from separating.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.846, including dough strengthener and emulsifier uses with specified limits.

entries.name: Calcium stearoyl lactylate
entries.what: The calcium salt analog of SSL, used as a dough strengthener and emulsifier in some baked products.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Same manufacturing job as SSL, with a slightly different handling and dough feel.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.844.

entries.name: Polysorbate 80
entries.what: A synthetic emulsifier used to keep oil and water mixed in ice cream, dressings, pickles, vitamins, and some sauces.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is very efficient at low use levels, so a plant can keep a smooth texture in a frozen dessert or a cloudy drink without a large amount of egg yolk or mustard.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.840, with specified foods and maximum levels. Related polysorbates are at 172.836 (60), 172.838 (65), and 172.842 (20) in adjacent sections.

entries.name: Polysorbate 60
entries.what: A synthetic emulsifier, similar to polysorbate 80, often used in cakes, icings, and whipped toppings.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It helps a cake mix or a whipped topping hold air and stay uniform after mixing or freezing.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.836, with specified uses and limits.

entries.name: Polysorbate 20
entries.what: A synthetic emulsifier used in some flavor emulsions and other listed uses, generally at low levels.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It helps a flavor oil stay dispersed in a water-based beverage or a flavor concentrate.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.515 (as a flavor adjuvant in some uses) and related sections; see also neighboring polysorbate listings.

entries.name: Sorbitan monostearate
entries.what: An emulsifier often used with a polysorbate in cakes, icings, and chocolate coatings.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Paired with a more water-loving emulsifier, it helps a cake or coating stay evenly mixed and hold its structure.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.842.

entries.name: PGPR
aliases: polyglycerol esters of interesterified ricinoleic acid
entries.what: An emulsifier used in chocolate and compound coatings to thin the chocolate so it can be pumped and molded with less cocoa butter.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A little PGPR lowers the viscosity of chocolate, which lets a plant coat and mold more easily and often with less expensive fat.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.856.

entries.name: Sucrose esters
entries.what: Emulsifiers made by attaching fatty acids to sucrose, used in some baked goods, dairy analogs, and chewing gum.
entries.why_plants_use_it: They can stabilize a foam or an emulsion in formulas where a plant wants a sucrose-based rather than a glycerol-based emulsifier.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.859.

entries.name: Propylene glycol alginate
entries.what: An alginate that has been reacted with propylene glycol, used as a stabilizer and emulsifier in salad dressings, beer foam, and sauces.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It holds a dressing together in acid conditions that would break some other gums, and it can stabilize foam.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.858.

entries.name: Brominated vegetable oil
entries.what: A weighting agent once used so citrus flavor oils would stay suspended in some sodas instead of floating. FDA has revoked the food-additive regulation authorizing it.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Citrus oils are lighter than the drink. BVO made the oil droplet dense enough to stay mixed. Plants are reformulating with other weighting agents or emulsion systems.
entries.regulatory_note: FDA revoked the regulation authorizing BVO in food (effective date in 2024, with a compliance period into 2025). It should no longer be used in US food; older stock is being cleared.

fmg_reveals.title: Gatorade used to have brominated vegetable oil in it, BVO, which is patented as a flame retardant and was banned in Europe and Japan
fmg_reveals.finding: Gatorade used to have brominated vegetable oil in it, BVO, which is patented as a flame retardant and was banned in Europe and Japan. A 15 year old named Sarah Kavanagh read the label in 2012, looked it up, and started a petition that got 200,000 signatures.

entries.name: Modified food starch
entries.what: Starch from corn, potato, tapioca, or wheat that has been treated (chemically, physically, or enzymatically) so it thickens more reliably under heat, acid, shear, or freeze-thaw.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Native starch can break down when you cook it, freeze it, or make the formula acidic. A modified starch holds a sauce, a coating, a filling, or a batter together through the plant and the warehouse. US labels usually do not say which starch or which treatment.
entries.regulatory_note: Food starch-modified is listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.892, which describes permitted treatments. The label term is typically 'food starch-modified' or 'modified food starch' and need not name the treatment.

fmg_reveals.finding: Burger King fries are coated in a batter. McDonald's fries aren't.

fmg_reveals.title: Modified food starch is starch that was treated with a chemical
fmg_reveals.finding: Modified food starch is starch that was treated with a chemical. The label doesn't say which one.

entries.name: Corn starch
entries.what: The native starch of corn, used as a thickener, anti-caking agent, and dusting powder, and as the starting material for many corn sweeteners.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is cheap, bland, and thickens when cooked. A plant uses the unmodified form when the process is gentle enough that a modified starch is not needed.

fmg_reveals.title: The jelly bean in your candy bag took about a week to make
fmg_reveals.finding: The jelly bean in your candy bag took about a week to make. The center starts as a cooked mix of sugar, water, cornstarch and corn syrup.

fmg_reveals.title: Powdered sugar is about 3% cornstarch
fmg_reveals.finding: Powdered sugar is about 3% cornstarch. Domino says so on its own site, and the box lists it as sugar and cornstarch.

fmg_reveals.finding: Your strawberry Twizzlers have no licorice in them. The list is corn syrup, wheat flour, sugar and cornstarch, then palm oil, salt, artificial flavor, citric acid, mineral oil, Red 40 and soy lecithin at 2% or less.

entries.name: Tapioca starch
entries.what: Native starch from cassava, used as a thickener and in gluten-free baking, and as a starting material for tapioca syrup and modified tapioca starch.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It gives a clear, glossy gel and is useful when a plant wants a corn-free or gluten-free starch.

entries.name: Potato starch
entries.what: Native starch from potatoes, used as a thickener and in some batters, noodles, and gluten-free mixes.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It swells at a relatively low temperature and can give a tender bite in a batter or a noodle.

fmg_reveals.finding: Burger King fries are coated in a batter. McDonald's fries aren't.

fmg_reveals.title: Veggie Straws are potato starch
fmg_reveals.finding: Veggie Straws are potato starch. The vegetables are powders, and most of them are there for color.

entries.name: Xanthan gum
entries.what: A gum made by fermenting a sugar with Xanthomonas campestris. It thickens and stabilizes at very low use levels, including in gluten-free baking and in dressings that have to hang on a salad.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A little xanthan keeps particles suspended, gives a sauce cling, and replaces some of the structure that gluten or fat would have given.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.695.

fmg_reveals.finding: Burger King fries are coated in a batter. McDonald's fries aren't.

entries.name: Guar gum
entries.what: A gum from guar beans, used to thicken and bind water in ice cream, sauces, gluten-free baking, and some dairy spreads.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It hydrates in cold water and is relatively inexpensive, so a plant can thicken a product without cooking a starch.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1339.

fmg_reveals.title: The citric acid in a Celsius is grown by a mold, and the taurine was never near a bull

The list is carbonated water, citric acid, taurine, vegetable juice for color, guarana seed extract, green tea extract, caffeine, ascorbic acid, sucralose, glucuronolactone, ginger root extract and a vitamin pack.

fmg_reveals.title: The Philadelphia in the tub isn't cream cheese
fmg_reveals.finding: Cream cheese has a federal standard: at least 33% milkfat, no more than 55% moisture. Cream cheese spread has none.

entries.name: Locust bean gum
entries.what: A gum from carob (locust bean) seeds, often paired with carrageenan or xanthan in ice cream and cream cheese to control ice crystals and give body.
entries.why_plants_use_it: In combination with other gums it makes a smoother frozen dessert and a more spreadable soft cheese.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1343.

entries.name: Gellan gum
entries.what: A gum made by bacterial fermentation, used to suspend particles in beverages (for example, pulpy drinks) and to make some gels and plant-based products.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A very small amount can keep pulp or a fortificant suspended in a drink that would otherwise settle in the bottle.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.665.

entries.name: Gum arabic
entries.what: A gum from acacia trees, used to encapsulate flavors, stabilize beverage emulsions, and coat candies (including as a carrier on a Tic Tac-style product).
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is unusually good at holding a flavor oil in a spray-dried powder or a cloudy drink, and it gives a thin, crisp coat on a panned candy.

entries.name: Pectin

entries.name: Carrageenan
entries.what: A gum extracted from red seaweed. In a plant it is a thickener and stabilizer. It gels or keeps particles suspended, and it can give a low-fat liquid some of the body that fat would have given it.
entries.why_plants_use_it: When you take the fat out of a dairy product, you also take out the mouthfeel. Carrageenan is one of the cheap ways to put that back without putting the cream back. It is also used in some plant milks, deli meats, and desserts.

entries.name: Agar
entries.what: A gel-forming gum from red seaweed, used in some desserts, confectionery, and microbiology-adjacent food gels, including vegan alternatives to gelatin.

entries.name: Sodium alginate
entries.what: A gum from brown seaweed, used to thicken, to gel with calcium (including 'caviar' and some onion-ring batters), and to hold moisture in some foods.

entries.name: Cellulose
entries.what: Plant fiber, often from wood pulp or cotton, used as a powder to bulk a mix, keep grated cheese from clumping, or add fiber. It does not come from the food it is mixed into.

entries.name: Methylcellulose

entries.name: Gelatin

entries.name: Konjac gum

entries.name: Gum tragacanth

entries.name: Butter

entries.name: Tallow

entries.name: Fully hydrogenated oil

entries.name: Partially hydrogenated oil

entries.name: Interesterified oil
entries.what: A fat whose fatty acids have been rearranged on the glycerol backbone, chemically or with enzymes, to change the melt and hardness without partial hydrogenation.

fmg_reveals.title: Cap'N Crunch Berries have no berries in them
fmg_reveals.finding: Cap'N Crunch Berries have no berries in them. The ingredient list is corn flour, sugar, oat flour, palm or coconut oil, salt and molasses, then Red 40, Yellow 5, Blue 1, Yellow 6 and natural and artificial flavor.

fmg_reveals.title: Your strawberry Twizzlers have no licorice in them
fmg_reveals.finding: Your strawberry Twizzlers have no licorice in them. The list is corn syrup, wheat flour, sugar and cornstarch, then palm oil, salt, artificial flavor, citric acid, mineral oil, Red 40 and soy lecithin at 2% or less.

fmg_reveals.title: There is no maple in Mrs. Butterworth's
fmg_reveals.finding: There is no maple in Mrs. Butterworth's. The ingredient list is high fructose corn syrup, corn syrup, water, and under 2% of cellulose gum, salt, molasses, natural and artificial flavor, caramel color, and preservatives.

entries.name: Spices
entries.what: A labeling category for aromatic vegetable substances used to flavor food. A label may say 'spices' instead of naming each one, with some exceptions.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can protect a formula, save label space, and sometimes use the word as a broad heading. 'Spices' is not a preservative, though some spice extractives (for example rosemary) are used for antioxidant effect and should be thought of that way when that is the job.
entries.regulatory_note: Defined and declared under 21 CFR 101.22. The term 'spices' may be used for substances that meet that definition; onion, garlic, and celery may have additional declaration expectations depending on use. Allergens cannot be hidden in this term.

entries.name: Vanillin
entries.what: The main aroma compound of vanilla. It can come from the vanilla bean or be made by synthesis (including from lignin, guaiacol, or other processes). Ethyl vanillin is a close analog, usually synthetic, and is stronger.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Both 'pure vanilla extract' and 'imitation vanilla' get their characteristic smell from vanillin. Imitation is mostly the molecule plus a solvent; pure extract also contains the other compounds of the bean, and costs much more.
entries.regulatory_note: Vanillin is listed as GRAS among synthetic flavoring substances at 21 CFR 182.60. The standard of identity for vanilla extract is at 21 CFR 169.175; imitation vanilla is labeled under general flavor-labeling rules in 21 CFR 101.22.

fmg_reveals.title: The two bottles of vanilla share one molecule, and you pay for everything else
fmg_reveals.finding: Both pure extract and imitation get their smell from vanillin; a 2 oz pure bottle cost $6.99 and an 8 oz store-brand imitation $1.75 this week, about 16 times as much per ounce for pure.

fmg_reveals.title: Imitation vanilla beat pure extract in an America's Test Kitchen tasting
fmg_reveals.finding: America's Test Kitchen tasted vanillas stirred into pudding and frosting, and an imitation came out on top with a pure extract close behind; it won even where the vanilla wasn't cooked.

entries.name: MSG
entries.what: The sodium salt of glutamic acid, used as a flavor enhancer to increase savory (umami) taste. It can be made by fermenting a sugar with a bacterium.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A small amount makes a broth, a snack seasoning, or a soup taste meatier or more rounded without adding more meat or salt in the same way. Related ingredients (yeast extract, hydrolyzed proteins, inosinate, guanylate) can do a similar job.
entries.regulatory_note: Monosodium glutamate is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 182.1 context and is a declared ingredient; 21 CFR 101.22 requires that protein hydrolysates and autolyzed yeast be declared by their common or usual names, and MSG must be declared when it is added.

fmg_reveals.title: MSG is made by feeding sugar to a soil bacterium
fmg_reveals.finding: MSG is made by feeding sugar to a soil bacterium. At Ajinomoto's plant in Eddyville, Iowa, the sugar is glucose, and the company says it comes from Iowa corn.

entries.name: Yeast extract
entries.what: Yeast that has been broken down so that amino acids and nucleotides, including free glutamate, are available as a savory flavor. It is a common 'not listed as MSG' umami ingredient.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It builds a roasted, meaty, or cheesy note in soups, snacks, and plant-based meats. A plant can get a glutamate-type enhancement and list 'yeast extract' instead of MSG.
entries.regulatory_note: Autolyzed yeast and yeast extract must be declared by their common or usual names under 21 CFR 101.22. They are not declared as MSG, though they can contain free glutamate.

entries.name: Hydrolyzed vegetable protein
entries.what: Plant protein (often soy, corn, or wheat) that has been broken down with acid or enzymes into amino acids and small peptides, used as a savory flavor. Acid-hydrolyzed soy is also how some non-brewed 'soy sauce' is made.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is a fast way to get a roasted, soy-sauce-like, or meaty flavor. Non-brewed soy sauce can be made in a day this way, versus months for a brewed sauce.
entries.regulatory_note: Protein hydrolysates must be declared by a common or usual name that includes the food source, under 21 CFR 101.22. If the source is a major allergen (soy, wheat), allergen rules also apply.

fmg_reveals.title: Two products share the name soy sauce, and only one of them was brewed
fmg_reveals.finding: Brewed soy sauce is soybeans, wheat and salt fermented for months. Non-brewed soy sauce is hydrolyzed soy protein, acid, caramel color and corn syrup made in a day.

fmg_reveals.title: The soy sauce packet in your takeout bag isn't soy sauce
fmg_reveals.finding: The soy sauce packet in your takeout bag isn't soy sauce. The biggest maker, Kari-Out in New Jersey, lists water, salt, hydrolyzed soy and corn protein, caramel color and sodium benzoate.

entries.name: Disodium inosinate
entries.what: A nucleotide flavor enhancer, often used with MSG or with disodium guanylate, in snack seasonings, soups, and instant noodles.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Inosinate and guanylate amplify the umami effect of glutamate, so a plant can get more savory impact from a smaller amount of a seasoning blend.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.535.

entries.name: Disodium guanylate
entries.what: A nucleotide flavor enhancer, almost always paired with disodium inosinate and/or MSG in savory seasonings.
entries.why_plants_use_it: The combination with inosinate and glutamate is more effective than any one of them alone, which is why 'disodium inosinate and disodium guanylate' show up together at the end of a snack ingredient list.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.530.

entries.name: Salt
entries.what: Sodium chloride, the basic seasoning and a preservative in some foods. 'Sea salt' and 'kosher salt' are still sodium chloride, sometimes with a different crystal size or trace minerals, and often with an anti-caking agent.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It seasons, it controls water activity, it strengthens dough, and it is how a plant gets a product to taste 'finished.' A different name (sea salt) is often a label story, not a different chemical.

entries.name: Potassium chloride
entries.what: A salt substitute used to lower sodium in soups, snacks, and 'reduced sodium' products. It can taste bitter or metallic at high levels, so it is usually blended with sodium chloride.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant that has to hit a sodium target but still wants a salty taste uses KCl for part of the salt, often with flavor modifiers to cover the bitterness.

fmg_reveals.title: A serving of Campbell's tomato soup has more sugar than a Krispy Kreme glazed donut
fmg_reveals.finding: A serving of Campbell's tomato soup has more sugar than a Krispy Kreme glazed donut. The can lists tomato puree, water, wheat flour and sugar, then under 2% of salt, potassium salt, natural flavoring, citric acid, vitamin C, celery extract and garlic oil.

entries.name: Smoke flavor
entries.what: A flavor made by condensing wood smoke (or made to match it), used so a product can taste smoked without a long time in a smokehouse — or in addition to a short smoke.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is faster and more consistent than traditional smoking, and it can be added to a sauce, a snack, or a meat that never saw a smoker.
entries.regulatory_note: Smoke flavoring is addressed in FDA flavor-labeling rules (21 CFR 101.22) and, for meat and poultry, in FSIS labeling rules about 'smoked' versus 'smoke flavor added.'

fmg_reveals.title: The ingredient called hickory smoke flavor is wood smoke condensed into a liquid, minus the tar
fmg_reveals.finding: The ingredient called hickory smoke flavor is wood smoke condensed into a liquid, minus the tar. The EU is phasing it out.

entries.name: Caffeine
entries.what: A stimulant added to some sodas, energy drinks, and 'energy' snack products, and naturally present in coffee and tea. When it is added, it should be declared as an ingredient.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant adds it when the product's purpose includes an alertness or 'energy' positioning, at a consistent dose.
entries.regulatory_note: Caffeine is listed as GRAS for use in cola-type beverages at 21 CFR 182.1180, at a maximum of 0.02 percent. Other added-caffeine uses are evaluated case by case; added caffeine in some foods has been the subject of FDA attention.

entries.name: Citric acid
entries.what: A tart acid, today almost always made by fermenting a sugar with a mold (Aspergillus niger), used to acidify, chelate metals, and brighten flavor. Sodium or potassium citrate is the buffered salt.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it to set pH, to keep a fruit flavor sharp, to help a preservative work, and to keep metals from causing haze or oxidation. The salt forms (citrates) buffer the acid so a drink is tart but not harsh.
entries.regulatory_note: Citric acid is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1033. Sodium citrate is at 21 CFR 184.1751.

fmg_reveals.title: Snapple Peach Tea has no peach on the ingredient list
fmg_reveals.finding: Snapple Peach Tea has no peach on the ingredient list. It reads filtered water, sugar, citric acid, tea and natural flavors, with the tea listed after the citric acid.

fmg_reveals.title: The citric acid in your food is grown on a black mold
fmg_reveals.finding: The citric acid in your food is grown on a black mold. Pfizer figured out how to mass produce it and it's how Pfizer learned to make penicillin.

fmg_reveals.title: The citric acid in a Celsius is grown by a mold, and the taurine was never near a bull
fmg_reveals.finding: The citric acid in a Celsius is grown by a mold, and the taurine was never near a bull. The list is carbonated water, citric acid, taurine, vegetable juice for color, guarana seed extract, green tea extract, caffeine, ascorbic acid, sucralose, glucuronolactone, ginger root extract and a vitamin pack.
