fmg_reveals.title: Land O Lakes Fat Free Half & Half is mostly skim milk and corn syrup
fmg_reveals.finding: Land O Lakes Fat Free Half & Half is mostly skim milk and corn syrup. The carton lists skim milk, corn syrup and cream, then 0.5% or less of carrageenan, sodium citrate, dipotassium phosphate, mono and diglycerides, vitamin A palmitate and color added.

fmg_reveals.title: Your strawberry Twizzlers have no licorice in them
fmg_reveals.finding: Your strawberry Twizzlers have no licorice in them. The list is corn syrup, wheat flour, sugar and cornstarch, then palm oil, salt, artificial flavor, citric acid, mineral oil, Red 40 and soy lecithin at 2% or less.

entries.name: Malic acid
entries.what: A tart acid that occurs in apples and other fruit, used in candies, drinks, and sour snacks because its tartness lingers longer than citric acid.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It gives a longer sour note, which is useful in 'sour' candy and in apple- or berry-flavored drinks.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1069.

entries.name: Lactic acid
entries.what: An acid produced by fermentation, used to acidify foods, to flavor (a mild tang), and, as lactate salts, to help preserve meat.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is the tang of yogurt and of some pickles and cured meats. A plant can lower pH and add a dairy-adjacent flavor without adding dairy.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1061.

entries.name: Acetic acid
entries.what: The acid in vinegar. On labels you will usually see 'vinegar' or 'distilled vinegar,' and sometimes 'acetic acid' in more technical formulas.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It acidifies, preserves, and flavors pickles, sauces, and dressings. Powdered vinegar is the same acid on a carrier.
entries.regulatory_note: Acetic acid is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1005. Vinegar is a food with a common or usual name rather than a numbered food additive.

fmg_reveals.title: Worcestershire sauce is a fish sauce
fmg_reveals.finding: Worcestershire sauce is a fish sauce. The Lea & Perrins bottle reads distilled white vinegar, molasses, sugar, water, salt, onions, anchovies, garlic, cloves, tamarind extract, natural flavorings and chili pepper extract.

fmg_reveals.title: Duke's mayonnaise has no sugar in it, and Hellmann's and Kraft both do
fmg_reveals.finding: Duke's mayonnaise has no sugar in it, and Hellmann's and Kraft both do. Duke's lists soybean oil, eggs, water, distilled and cider vinegar, salt, oleoresin paprika, natural flavors and calcium disodium EDTA.

fmg_reveals.title: Honey. Salt. Sugar. White rice. Dried beans. Vinegar. Anything over 40 proof
fmg_reveals.finding: Honey. Salt. Sugar. White rice. Dried beans. Vinegar. Anything over 40 proof. Brown rice has natural oils and will spoil.

entries.name: Phosphoric acid
entries.what: A mineral acid used to acidify colas and some other drinks, and as a starting point for phosphate salts used in meat, cheese, and leavening.
entries.why_plants_use_it: In a cola it gives a sharp bite that citric acid does not, and it is cheap and consistent at beverage scale.

entries.name: Tartaric acid
entries.what: An acid from grapes (or made to match it), used in some baking, candies, and as the parent of cream of tartar.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It gives a sharp, clean tartness and is the acid part of some baking powders and cream-of-tartar systems.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1099.

entries.name: Fumaric acid
entries.what: A tart, relatively non-hygroscopic acid used in some dry beverage mixes, tortillas, and candies because it stays dry in a powder.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It gives sourness in a dry mix that has to flow freely and not cake in the packet.

entries.name: Adipic acid
entries.what: A food acid used in some drink powders and gelatin desserts for a tart taste and a dry, free-flowing powder.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Similar job to fumaric acid in dry mixes: tartness without pulling in as much moisture as citric acid would.

entries.name: Glucono delta-lactone
entries.what: A slow-release acidulant that gradually converts to gluconic acid in water, used in some cheeses, tofu, cured meats, and baking.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It lowers pH gradually, which is useful when a plant wants a gentle set (tofu, some sausages) rather than an instant sour hit.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1318.

entries.name: Sodium phosphates
entries.what: A family of phosphate salts used to hold water in meat and shrimp, to buffer pH, to emulsify cheese sauces, and as leavening acids. The label may say sodium phosphate, sodium tripolyphosphate, dipotassium phosphate, and several other names.
entries.why_plants_use_it: In meat or shrimp, phosphates help the protein hold injected or absorbed water so the product stays plump and juicy after cooking. In a cheese sauce, they help the cheese stay smooth. In a baked good, some phosphates are the acid in baking powder.
entries.regulatory_note: Many phosphate salts are listed as GRAS, for example sodium acid pyrophosphate at 21 CFR 182.1087 and sodium phosphate at related 182.1778-type listings. Use in meat and poultry also falls under FSIS rules, including limits on added solution and required labeling of injected product.

fmg_reveals.title: The pork chops at the meat counter were injected with solution
fmg_reveals.finding: The pork chops at the meat counter were injected with solution. The tray reads up to 12% solution of water, salt and sodium phosphate.

fmg_reveals.title: Great Value frozen shrimp has 3 ingredients
fmg_reveals.finding: Great Value frozen shrimp has 3 ingredients. Shrimp, salt and sodium tripolyphosphate.

fmg_reveals.title: Land O Lakes Fat Free Half & Half is mostly skim milk and corn syrup
fmg_reveals.finding: Land O Lakes Fat Free Half & Half is mostly skim milk and corn syrup. The carton lists skim milk, corn syrup and cream, then 0.5% or less of carrageenan, sodium citrate, dipotassium phosphate, mono and diglycerides, vitamin A palmitate and color added.

entries.name: Ascorbic acid
entries.what: Vitamin C, used as a nutrient, as an antioxidant, as a dough oxidizer, and as a cure accelerator in meat (sometimes as sodium ascorbate or erythorbate).
entries.why_plants_use_it: One ingredient can do several jobs: keep a fruit color, help a cured-meat reaction, strengthen a dough, and support a vitamin C claim.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 182.3013 (preservative) and 182.8013 (nutrient), among other listings.

fmg_reveals.title: Martinelli's sparkling cider is apple juice with bubbles in it
fmg_reveals.finding: The ingredients are pasteurized 100% carbonated apple juice from US grown fresh apples and vitamin C, and the bottle says it contains no water, alcohol or sweeteners.

fmg_reveals.title: Most of the vitamin C the US imports comes from China
fmg_reveals.finding: Most of the vitamin C the US imports comes from China. In 2025 it was 88% by weight, about 95 million pounds.

fmg_reveals.title: The citric acid in a Celsius is grown by a mold, and the taurine was never near a bull
fmg_reveals.finding: The citric acid in a Celsius is grown by a mold, and the taurine was never near a bull. The list is carbonated water, citric acid, taurine, vegetable juice for color, guarana seed extract, green tea extract, caffeine, ascorbic acid, sucralose, glucuronolactone, ginger root extract and a vitamin pack.

fmg_reveals.title: A serving of Campbell's tomato soup has more sugar than a Krispy Kreme glazed donut
fmg_reveals.finding: A serving of Campbell's tomato soup has more sugar than a Krispy Kreme glazed donut. The can lists tomato puree, water, wheat flour and sugar, then under 2% of salt, potassium salt, natural flavoring, citric acid, vitamin C, celery extract and garlic oil.

entries.name: Baking soda
entries.what: A simple alkaline leavening salt. It releases carbon dioxide when it meets an acid and moisture, or when it is heated.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is the base of almost every chemical leavening system. A plant pairs it with an acid (cream of tartar, a phosphate, GDL) so gas is released at the right time in the oven or on the griddle.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1736.

entries.name: Baking powder
entries.what: A complete chemical leavening blend: baking soda plus one or more acids, and usually a starch to keep it dry. 'Double-acting' powders release some gas when wet and more when heated.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A mix or a plant bakery can get a consistent rise without yeast time. The acid package is chosen so the gas comes off at the right stage of mixing and baking.

fmg_reveals.title: Clabber Girl baking powder has aluminum in it
fmg_reveals.finding: Clabber Girl baking powder has aluminum in it. So do most of the store brands next to it.

entries.name: Monocalcium phosphate
entries.what: A fast-acting leavening acid that reacts with baking soda as soon as it gets wet, used in some baking powders and pancake mixes.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It gives an early rise in the bowl or on a griddle, often paired with a slower acid for a second rise in the oven.
entries.regulatory_note: Calcium phosphate, monobasic, is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 182.1217.

entries.name: Sodium acid pyrophosphate
entries.what: A delayed-action leavening acid used in doughnuts, refrigerated doughs, and some frozen batters, and also as a color-protection agent in some potatoes.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It can be manufactured to release gas later in the process, which is useful in a dough that has to sit in a tube or a freezer before it is baked.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 182.1087.

entries.name: Sodium aluminum phosphate
entries.what: A slow-acting leavening acid used in some baking powders, refrigerated doughs, and cakes, so most of the gas is released in the oven rather than in the bowl.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A refrigerated dough or a cake mix that has to sit needs a leavening acid that will not spend itself too early.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 182.1781.

entries.name: Cream of tartar
entries.what: A leavening acid and stabilizer, the potassium salt of tartaric acid, used with baking soda and to stabilize egg whites.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is a familiar, relatively gentle acid for a home-style baking powder and for whipped whites that need to hold a foam.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1077.

entries.name: Ammonium bicarbonate
entries.what: A leavening salt that fully decomposes into gases in a hot, thin cookie or cracker, leaving little or no residual salt in the crumb.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is useful in dry, thin baked goods (spritz cookies, crackers) where a phosphate-soda system might leave a taste or a thicker crumb.

entries.name: Yeast (leavening)
entries.what: Living (or dried living) yeast used to leaven bread and to ferment some flavors. It is an ingredient, not a chemical baking powder.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It produces carbon dioxide and flavor over time. A plant bakery may still use dough conditioners and enzymes so a yeasted dough can run on a clock.

entries.name: Silicon dioxide
entries.what: A mineral anti-caking agent used so powders — spices, coffee creamers, drink mixes, shredded cheese in some cases — flow instead of clumping.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A dry mix has to go through a filler and then out of a consumer jar. A small amount of silica keeps it free-flowing in humid conditions.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.480, with a maximum use as an anti-caking agent generally not to exceed 2 percent of the food.

entries.name: Calcium silicate
entries.what: A mineral anti-caking agent used in some salts, spices, and baking powders.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Same job as silicon dioxide: keep a powder from setting up into a cake in the package.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.410.

fmg_reveals.title: There's sugar in Morton table salt
fmg_reveals.finding: There's sugar in Morton table salt. The ingredients on the iodized canister are salt, calcium silicate, dextrose and potassium iodide.

entries.name: Sodium aluminosilicate
entries.what: A mineral anti-caking agent often used in table salt, drink mixes, and powdered mixes.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is a common reason a salt still pours in humid weather.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 182.2727.

entries.name: Tricalcium phosphate
entries.what: A calcium phosphate used as an anti-caking agent and as a calcium source in some powders and non-dairy creamers.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It can do two jobs at once: keep a powder flowing and add calcium for a nutrition claim.

entries.name: Magnesium stearate
entries.what: A fatty-acid salt used as an anti-caking and flow agent, and as a lubricant in some tablet-like compressed foods and supplements.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It helps a powder or a compressed product release from equipment and not stick to itself.

fmg_reveals.title: A Tic Tac is mostly sugar, and the box says 0 calories and 0 carbohydrate
fmg_reveals.finding: A Tic Tac is mostly sugar, and the box says 0 calories and 0 carbohydrate. Sugar is the first ingredient, then maltodextrin, rice starch, gum arabic, flavors, magnesium stearate and carnauba wax.

entries.name: Yellow prussiate of soda
entries.what: An anti-caking agent used at very low levels in some table salts.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It keeps salt crystals from caking in the shaker or the bulk bag.

entries.name: L-cysteine
entries.what: An amino acid used as a dough relaxer so bread and tortilla doughs are easier to extend and machine. Historically, much of the L-cysteine used in dough has been made from animal feathers or hair; vegetarian fermentation sources also exist.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A tight dough fights a high-speed line. L-cysteine relaxes the gluten so a plant can sheet, stamp, or twist it without tearing, in less time.

fmg_reveals.title: Much of the L-cysteine in bread dough has been made from feathers and hair
fmg_reveals.finding: Much of the L-cysteine in bread dough has been made from feathers and hair.

entries.name: Azodicarbonamide
entries.what: A dough conditioner and a bleaching agent for cereal flour, used so a dough handles more easily and a flour looks whiter. It has been restricted or banned in some other countries and in some US states; it remains listed in federal FDA regulations unless those rules are changed.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It gives a plant tighter control over dough strength and flour color on a high-speed bakery line.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.806, with maximum use levels in flour and in bread dough. Some US states have enacted their own restrictions; check current state law as well as the federal listing.

entries.name: Calcium peroxide
entries.what: An oxidizing dough conditioner used in some breads to strengthen gluten and improve dough handling.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Oxidizing agents help a dough hold gas and give a more uniform crumb on a commercial line.
entries.regulatory_note: Used as a dough conditioner in cereal flours and bread under FDA food-additive listings (see 21 CFR Part 172, flour-treating agents). Check the specific listing for use levels.

entries.name: Potassium bromate
entries.what: An oxidizing dough conditioner and flour improver. It is still listed in federal FDA regulations for certain bread and flour uses, but it has been largely abandoned by many US bakers, is banned in some other countries, and is restricted by some US states. A label that still says 'bromated flour' is telling you it is in the flour.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It strengthens dough and can give a higher rise. Many plants have switched to ascorbic acid or other conditioners because of regulatory and customer pressure.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.730, with residual limits in finished bread. Some states restrict or require warnings; the federal listing has not been a complete US ban as of the sources used here. Always check current FDA and state rules.

fmg_reveals.title: Potassium bromate makes dough stronger and rise higher
fmg_reveals.finding: Potassium bromate makes dough stronger and rise higher. It's been banned in the EU and UK since 1990, Canada since 1994, China since 2005, and more than two dozen countries in total.

entries.name: Enzymes (dough and food)
entries.what: A catch-all label term for protein catalysts used to break down starch, protein, or fat, to extend freshness, or to help a dough handle. The label may just say 'enzymes' or may name amylase, protease, and others.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can get a softer loaf that stays soft longer, a cracker that sheets cleanly, or a juice that is clearer, without a long traditional process. Many enzymes are inactivated by baking or pasteurization and are treated as processing aids in some uses, but they still often appear on ingredient lists.
entries.regulatory_note: Many enzyme preparations are listed in 21 CFR Part 173 (secondary direct food additives) or are the subject of GRAS notices. Declaration depends on whether the enzyme is a food ingredient with a technical effect in the finished food or a processing aid; 21 CFR 101.100 addresses some processing-aid exemptions.

entries.name: Amylase
entries.what: An enzyme that breaks starch into smaller sugars. In baking it feeds yeast and can keep bread softer for longer (especially maltogenic amylase).
entries.why_plants_use_it: A commercial loaf that has to stay soft for a week often relies on an amylase rather than only on emulsifiers and shortening.

entries.name: Protease
entries.what: An enzyme that breaks down protein. In baking it relaxes dough; in meat it can tenderize; papain and bromelain are familiar plant proteases.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it to make a dough extensible, to clear a protein haze, or to tenderize a meat, depending on the product.

entries.name: Transglutaminase
entries.what: An enzyme that cross-links proteins, used to bind pieces of meat or fish, to improve the texture of some yogurts and plant-based proteins, and in some baking.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It lets a plant make a uniform portion from smaller pieces, or give a softer protein network a firmer bite, without a lot of added binder.

entries.name: Rennet
entries.what: The enzyme used to coagulate milk into cheese curd. Today much US cheese is made with fermentation-produced chymosin rather than calf rennet.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It gives a clean, controlled curd set at plant scale. Fermentation-produced chymosin is consistent and does not depend on a calf-rennet supply.

entries.name: Lactase
entries.what: An enzyme that splits lactose into glucose and galactose, used to make lactose-free milk and some other dairy products.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It lets a plant sell a 'lactose-free' dairy product that still tastes like milk, with the lactose already broken down in the vat or in the pack.

entries.name: Whey protein concentrate
entries.what: The liquid protein fraction left when cheese is made, concentrated so that protein is a large share (but not all) of the powder. It still contains some lactose and fat.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is a relatively inexpensive dairy protein for shakes, bars, baked goods, and 'added protein' foods, and it still has some of the functional properties of whey.

fmg_reveals.title: The protein number on your tub of whey is a nitrogen count
fmg_reveals.finding: The protein number on your tub of whey is a nitrogen count. The lab digests the sample and measures the nitrogen.

entries.name: Whey protein isolate
entries.what: Whey protein that has been processed further so it is very high in protein and low in lactose and fat.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it when it wants a high protein claim, a clearer drink, or a lower lactose load than a concentrate would give.

entries.name: Milk protein concentrate
entries.what: A powder made by concentrating the proteins of milk (casein plus whey), used in cheeses, yogurts, bars, and processed dairy.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It lets a plant add dairy protein and some of milk's structure without adding as much lactose or water.

fmg_reveals.title: The cheese sauce in Kraft Macaroni & Cheese doesn't list cheese
fmg_reveals.finding: The cheese sauce in Kraft Macaroni & Cheese doesn't list cheese. The blue box packet is whey, milkfat, salt, milk protein concentrate and sodium triphosphate, then under 2% of starch, acids, paprika, turmeric and annatto for color, enzymes and cheese culture.

fmg_reveals.title: Ensure's biggest ingredient after water doesn't count as sugar on the label
fmg_reveals.finding: Ensure's biggest ingredient after water doesn't count as sugar on the label. It's corn maltodextrin, then sugar, then milk protein concentrate, vegetable oil and soy protein.

entries.name: Micellar casein
entries.what: Casein in its native micelle form, concentrated from milk. It is the slow-digesting dairy protein and is also used to add dairy character to some non-dairy-looking formulas (including some creamers).
entries.why_plants_use_it: A small amount can give a dairy note or a protein boost. In a 'non-dairy' creamer it may still appear in the under-2% group because casein is a milk protein.
entries.regulatory_note: Caseinates and milk proteins must be declared; they are milk allergens under FALCPA even when the front of the pack says 'non-dairy' in some older usages. FDA has addressed 'non-dairy' products that contain caseinate.

fmg_reveals.title: Coffee-mate Original has no cream in it
fmg_reveals.finding: Coffee-mate Original has no cream in it. The bottle is water, corn syrup solids and soybean oil, and the only dairy is micellar casein, a milk protein, in the under 2% group.

fmg_reveals.title: Coffee-mate costs less to make than half-and-half
fmg_reveals.finding: There is no cream in Coffee-mate. The bottle is water, corn syrup solids and soybean oil.

entries.name: Sodium caseinate
entries.what: Casein that has been converted to a soluble salt so it can be used as a protein and an emulsifier in coffee creamers, processed meats, and whipped toppings.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It helps a creamer or a topping stay mixed and adds dairy protein without using fluid milk as the base.
entries.regulatory_note: Sodium caseinate is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 182.1748. It is a milk allergen and must be declared.

entries.name: Soy protein isolate
entries.what: Soy protein that has been processed to a very high protein content, used in bars, meat analogs, beverages, and as a binder in some processed meats.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is a concentrated, relatively inexpensive protein that also binds water and fat, which is useful in a burger analog or a formed meat.

entries.name: Soy protein concentrate
entries.what: Soy protein with some of the soluble carbohydrates removed. Textured versions (TVP/TSP) are extruded to look like crumbs or chunks of meat.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it to extend meat, to build a meat analog, or to add protein and chew at a lower cost than muscle meat.

entries.name: Pea protein
entries.what: Protein extracted from yellow peas, used in plant-based meats, shakes, and 'dairy-free' products.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is a soy-free, dairy-free protein that can be extruded into a meat-like texture or blended into a beverage, which is useful for allergen-positioned products.

fmg_reveals.title: Goodles gets its 14 g of protein by stirring protein powder into the pasta
fmg_reveals.finding: Goodles gets its 14 g of protein by stirring protein powder into the pasta.

fmg_reveals.title: The Texas Roadhouse honey cinnamon butter at the grocery store has no butter in it
fmg_reveals.finding: The Texas Roadhouse honey cinnamon butter at the grocery store has no butter in it. The tub reads soybean oil, water, honey, palm oil, palm kernel oil, salt, cinnamon, soy lecithin, monoglycerides, pea protein, preservatives, natural flavors and beta carotene for color.

entries.name: Wheat protein
entries.what: The gluten proteins of wheat, concentrated and used to strengthen dough or to make meat analogs (seitan).
entries.why_plants_use_it: In bread it boosts protein and chew; in a meat analog it provides the fibrous bite. It is a wheat allergen and is not gluten-free.

fmg_reveals.title: Goodles gets its 14 g of protein by stirring protein powder into the pasta
fmg_reveals.finding: Goodles gets its 14 g of protein by stirring protein powder into the pasta.

entries.name: Chickpea protein
entries.what: Protein from chickpeas, used in some plant-based and allergen-positioned foods as an alternative to soy or pea.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can add protein and a different flavor base, and can market a pulse-based ingredient.

fmg_reveals.title: Goodles gets its 14 g of protein by stirring protein powder into the pasta
fmg_reveals.finding: Goodles gets its 14 g of protein by stirring protein powder into the pasta.

entries.name: Collagen
entries.what: Animal connective-tissue protein, often hydrolyzed into peptides for drinks and bars, or used as gelatin when it still gels.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is used for a protein claim, a 'skin, hair, and nails' positioning, or, as gelatin, for gelling. It is not a complete protein in the same amino-acid balance as whey or soy.

entries.name: Egg white protein
entries.what: The protein of egg whites, used as a binder, foaming agent, and protein ingredient in baking, pasta, and some processed meats and bars.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It sets with heat and holds air, which is useful in a binder or a foam, and it carries an egg allergen label.

entries.name: Inulin
entries.what: A soluble fiber, usually from chicory root, used to add fiber, to replace some sugar or fat, and to add a slight sweetness. Oligofructose (FOS) is a closely related shorter-chain material.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can raise the fiber number on the Nutrition Facts panel, improve body in a 'light' yogurt or bar, and use a plant-root name on the label.
entries.regulatory_note: Inulin and oligofructose are used under GRAS notices. FDA's fiber definition and isolated-fiber policy (21 CFR 101.9) affect whether a fiber may be counted as Dietary Fiber on the label.

entries.name: Polydextrose
entries.what: A synthetic polymer of glucose used as a bulking agent and soluble fiber in reduced-sugar and reduced-calorie foods.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It replaces some of the bulk that sugar or fat would have provided, so a 'light' ice cream or candy still has body.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.841. Whether it may be declared as Dietary Fiber depends on FDA's fiber definition and any petitioned uses.

entries.name: Soluble corn fiber
entries.what: A soluble fiber made from corn starch (often a resistant maltodextrin), used to add fiber and some bulk to drinks, bars, and 'high fiber' products with little viscosity.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Unlike some gums, it does not turn a drink into a gel at typical use levels, so a plant can raise fiber without changing the texture much.
entries.regulatory_note: Used under GRAS notices. Counting it as Dietary Fiber on the Nutrition Facts label depends on FDA's isolated-fiber policy under 21 CFR 101.9.

entries.name: Oat fiber
entries.what: A mostly insoluble fiber from oat hulls or oats, used to add fiber and some structure to baked goods and bars.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It boosts the fiber number and can help a cookie or a bread hold together with less flour.

entries.name: Bamboo fiber
entries.what: An insoluble cellulose-type fiber from bamboo, used as a bulking agent in some processed foods.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is another way to add non-caloric bulk and a fiber number, similar in manufacturing role to powdered cellulose.

entries.name: Psyllium husk
entries.what: A soluble, highly water-absorbing fiber from psyllium seed husks, used in some cereals, fiber supplements, and gluten-free baking.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It forms a gel and can stand in for some of the structure that gluten or eggs would have provided, and it supports a fiber claim.

entries.name: Resistant starch
entries.what: Starch that resists digestion in the small intestine, used to add fiber and to lower the digestible-carbohydrate contribution of a flour or a snack.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can replace some regular flour or starch, raise fiber, and sometimes support a lower-glycemic positioning, depending on the type and the label rules.

entries.name: Vitamin A palmitate
entries.what: A form of vitamin A added to milk, creamers, cereals, and some 'fat-free' dairy so the product meets a vitamin A level after the fat (and its natural vitamin A) has been removed, or to support a fortification claim.
entries.why_plants_use_it: When a plant skims fat, it also skims fat-soluble vitamins. Adding palmitate puts vitamin A back at a consistent level.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1930. Milk fortification practices are also addressed in the milk standards and in 21 CFR 131.

fmg_reveals.title: Land O Lakes Fat Free Half & Half is mostly skim milk and corn syrup
fmg_reveals.finding: Land O Lakes Fat Free Half & Half is mostly skim milk and corn syrup. The carton lists skim milk, corn syrup and cream, then 0.5% or less of carrageenan, sodium citrate, dipotassium phosphate, mono and diglycerides, vitamin A palmitate and color added.

entries.name: Vitamin D3
entries.what: The form of vitamin D most often added to milk, plant milks, cereals, and orange juice. D3 (cholecalciferol) is typically from lanolin (sheep's wool) or from lichen in some vegan grades; D2 is a plant/fungal form.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant adds it to hit a consistent IU level and to support a nutrition claim, especially in products that stand in for milk.
entries.regulatory_note: Vitamin D is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1950, with use limitations, and as a food additive in some additional uses (21 CFR 172.380 for some products).

fmg_reveals.title: The vitamin D3 added to milk is usually made from sheep's wool
fmg_reveals.finding: The vitamin D3 added to milk is usually made from sheep's wool. The NIH's fact sheet on vitamin D says D3 is "typically produced with irradiation of 7-dehydrocholesterol from lanolin obtained from the wool of sheep." Lanolin is the grease in wool.

entries.name: Thiamine mononitrate
entries.what: Vitamin B1, added to enriched flour, cereals, and some other grain products as part of the standard enrichment package.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Enrichment puts back (and standardizes) vitamins that were lost when the grain was milled. A plant making 'enriched' bread or pasta uses this as part of that legal package.
entries.regulatory_note: Thiamine mononitrate is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1878. Enrichment of flour and related products is set out in 21 CFR Part 137 and related standards.

entries.name: Riboflavin
entries.what: Vitamin B2, part of the flour-enrichment package, and also listed as a yellow color (see Riboflavin (color)).
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is added to enriched grains for the nutrient standard, and it can also tint a food slightly yellow.
entries.regulatory_note: Used as a nutrient under GRAS listings and in the enrichment standards in 21 CFR Part 137. As a color, see 21 CFR 73.450.

entries.name: Niacinamide
entries.what: Vitamin B3, part of the standard enrichment package for flour, rice, and many breakfast cereals.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Same enrichment job as thiamine and riboflavin: hit a legal or claimed nutrient level in a refined grain product.
entries.regulatory_note: Niacinamide is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1535. Enrichment standards are in 21 CFR Part 137.

entries.name: Folic acid
entries.what: The synthetic form of folate added to enriched grains and some other foods. In the US, enriched cereal-grain products are required to be fortified with folic acid.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is added at a standard level to enriched flour, bread, pasta, and rice. A plant making those products does not have a choice if it wants to use the 'enriched' standard.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a food additive at 21 CFR 172.345. Mandatory folic acid fortification of enriched cereal grains is set out in the standards of identity in 21 CFR Parts 136, 137, and 139.

fmg_reveals.title: Frosted Mini-Wheats aren't vegetarian
fmg_reveals.finding: Frosted Mini-Wheats aren't vegetarian. The ingredients are whole grain wheat and sugar, then 2% or less of brown rice syrup and gelatin, plus iron and folic acid.

entries.name: Cyanocobalamin
entries.what: The form of vitamin B12 most often added to fortified cereals, plant milks, nutritional yeasts, and supplements.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant-based product has no natural B12 from animal sources, so a plant that wants a 'good source of B12' claim adds it.
entries.regulatory_note: Vitamin B12 is listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1945.

entries.name: Pyridoxine hydrochloride
entries.what: Vitamin B6, added to some cereals, bars, and drinks as part of a vitamin premix.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is included when a plant wants a broader B-vitamin claim than the legal grain-enrichment package alone would give.

entries.name: Reduced iron
entries.what: Forms of iron added to enriched flour, cereals, and some other foods. 'Reduced iron' and 'electrolytic iron' are elemental iron powders; ferrous sulfate and ferrous fumarate are iron salts.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Iron is part of the US enrichment package for flour and many cereals. The form is chosen for color, taste, and bioavailability in that food.
entries.regulatory_note: Enrichment standards in 21 CFR Parts 136–139 specify iron as part of the enrichment package. Individual iron salts have GRAS or food-additive listings (for example ferrous sulfate at 21 CFR 184.1315).

entries.name: Zinc oxide
entries.what: A form of zinc added to some cereals, nutrition drinks, and other fortified foods.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is an inexpensive, stable way to hit a zinc daily-value claim in a premix.

entries.name: Potassium iodide
entries.what: The iodine source in iodized table salt, and in some other fortified foods. Potassium iodate is used in some bread-improver systems as well.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Iodized salt is a public-health fortification. A plant that uses non-iodized salt in a processed food is not delivering that iodine unless it adds it another way.

fmg_reveals.title: There's sugar in Morton table salt
fmg_reveals.finding: There's sugar in Morton table salt. The ingredients on the iodized canister are salt, calcium silicate, dextrose and potassium iodide.

entries.name: Calcium carbonate (fortificant)
entries.what: A calcium salt used to fortify plant milks, juices, cereals, and some baked goods, and also as a color and a pH-control agent.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is an inexpensive calcium source when a plant wants a 'good source of calcium' claim in a product that is not dairy, or in a dairy product whose calcium has been diluted.

entries.name: Methylene chloride
entries.what: A solvent used in some decaffeination processes and, historically, in other extractions. FDA has also addressed its use in fruit-stamping inks. Residues in decaf coffee are subject to limits.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It pulls caffeine out of the green bean efficiently. Other decaf methods use ethyl acetate, carbon dioxide, or water ('Swiss Water' and similar).
entries.regulatory_note: Methylene chloride is listed as an extraction solvent at 21 CFR 173.255, with residue limits, including for coffee. On November 9, 2026, FDA dropped it from the solvents allowed in fruit-stamping ink; the coffee solvent listing is a separate regulation and should be checked for any later amendments.

fmg_reveals.title: On November 9th the FDA dropped methylene chloride from the solvents allowed in fruit stamping ink
fmg_reveals.finding: On November 9th the FDA dropped methylene chloride from the solvents allowed in fruit stamping ink. It's still allowed in your decaf.

fmg_reveals.title: Most decaf coffee is made with methylene chloride
fmg_reveals.finding: Most decaf coffee is made with methylene chloride. It's the solvent that used to be in paint stripper.

entries.name: Ethyl acetate
entries.what: A solvent used in some 'naturally decaffeinated' coffee processes (it also occurs in fruit). Residues are subject to limits.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can market a solvent-decaffeinated coffee with a solvent that also exists in nature, as an alternative to methylene chloride.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as an extraction solvent at 21 CFR 173.228, with conditions and residue limits.

entries.name: Carbon dioxide (process)
entries.what: Carbon dioxide used as a supercritical extraction solvent (including some decaf and hop and flavor extracts), as a propellant, and as a carbonation gas.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It can extract caffeine or flavors without leaving a chlorinated-solvent residue, and it is also the bubble in a carbonated drink and a propellant in some cans.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1240.

entries.name: Hexane
entries.what: A solvent widely used to extract oil from soybeans and other oilseeds at industrial scale. It is a processing aid in the oil mill, not an ingredient a shopper should expect to see listed on a bottle of refined oil.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is an efficient way to get most of the oil out of a flake or a press cake. Refined oils are then desolventized; residual solvent is subject to limits.

entries.name: Dimethylpolysiloxane
entries.what: An antifoam and anti-spattering agent used in frying oils and in some cooking sprays (often listed next to the oil). It is a silicone, not a fat.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It keeps a fryer from foaming and can help a spray nozzle deliver a fine mist. In a cooking spray, it is one reason a '0 calorie' claim can still involve more than just the oil.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as a secondary direct food additive (defoaming agent) at 21 CFR 173.340, with conditions of use.

fmg_reveals.title: A can of PAM olive oil spray says 0 calories and 0 grams of fat
fmg_reveals.finding: A can of PAM olive oil spray says 0 calories and 0 grams of fat. The ingredients are extra virgin olive oil, soy lecithin and dimethyl silicone.

entries.name: Nitrous oxide
entries.what: A propellant used in whipped-cream cans (including dairy whipped cream and some toppings). The cream is not whipped until the gas is released at the nozzle.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It dissolves in the fat and then expands when the valve opens, which is how a can of whipping cream foams instantly.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1545, including use as a propellant.

fmg_reveals.title: Reddi-wip isn't whipped until you press the nozzle
fmg_reveals.finding: The can is filled with liquid cream and nitrous oxide gas under pressure, and the gas dissolves into the cream, especially the fat; pressing the nozzle drops the pressure.

entries.name: Nitrogen
entries.what: A gas used to flush snack bags and some other packages so there is less oxygen (which would go stale), and as a propellant in some sprays.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A bag of chips that is 'full of air' is usually full of nitrogen, which helps the product last and protects the chips in shipping.

entries.name: Bone char
entries.what: A traditional filter aid made from charred animal bones, still used by some refineries to decolorize cane sugar. It is a process aid at the refinery, not an ingredient listed on a bag of sugar. Beet sugar is not filtered this way; some cane sugars use other filters.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It is one way a refinery gets a very white crystal. It is also why some vegetarians look for beet sugar, unrefined cane sugar, or a brand that discloses an alternative filter.

fmg_reveals.title: Your white sugar could have been filtered through charred cattle bones
fmg_reveals.finding: Your white sugar could have been filtered through charred cattle bones. The label won’t tell you easily.

entries.name: Chlorine (wash)
entries.what: Chlorine or chlorine dioxide used as an antimicrobial wash on produce, poultry, and some other foods, and historically in flour treatment. These are processing treatments, usually not listed as ingredients on a bag of salad, subject to use rules.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant or a processor uses a wash to reduce microbes on a raw product that will be bagged and shipped. Labeling of the wash itself is often not required when it is a processing aid with no lasting technical effect.

entries.name: Natural
entries.what: A marketing claim that is only loosely defined for most FDA-regulated foods. FDA has a long-standing informal policy, not a full formal standard, that 'natural' means nothing artificial or synthetic has been added that would not normally be expected in the food. It is not a nutrient or safety claim.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it because shoppers treat it as a quality signal. It does not, by itself, ban many of the ingredients in this glossary, and it is not the same as 'organic.'
entries.regulatory_note: FDA has requested comments and has a policy statement on 'natural' but has not established a formal definition for most foods (see FDA's 'Use of the Term Natural on Food Labeling'). For meat and poultry, FSIS has a definition: a product that contains no artificial ingredients or added color and is only minimally processed, with a required explanatory statement.

entries.name: Organic
entries.what: A certified production and handling claim, administered by USDA's National Organic Program, not by a casual use of the word. '100% Organic,' 'Organic' (95%+), and 'Made with organic …' (70%+) have different rules and different allowed label treatments.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it when the ingredients and the supply chain are certified, because it commands a different shopper and often a different price. Organic still allows some processing and some added ingredients (including some sugars, gums, and ascorbic acid) from a limited national list.
entries.regulatory_note: Regulated at 7 CFR Part 205 (USDA AMS National Organic Program). Use of the USDA Organic seal is limited to products that meet the standard and are certified by an accredited certifier (with a narrow exemption for very small operations).

entries.name: Clean label
entries.what: A marketing phrase, not a legal claim. There is no FDA or USDA definition of 'clean label.' It usually means the plant is trying to use shorter, more kitchen-familiar ingredient names.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant reformulates from sodium nitrite to celery powder, from TBHQ to rosemary extract, from Red 40 to beet juice, or from 'artificial flavor' to 'natural flavor' so the list looks more like a pantry. The function of the ingredient is often the same.
entries.regulatory_note: Not defined in FDA or USDA labeling regulations. Claims still cannot be false or misleading under the FD&C Act or the FMIA/PPIA, but 'clean' itself has no standard of identity or nutrient rule.

entries.name: No added sugar
entries.what: A nutrient content claim with a specific legal test. It does not mean the food has no sugar — fruit, milk, and some other ingredients bring sugars of their own — and it does not automatically mean the food is low-calorie.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can sweeten with fruit, fruit-juice concentrate (with limits on the claim), or a non-sugar sweetener, or it can simply not add a sugar to a food that already tastes sweet. The Nutrition Facts panel is still where total and added sugars are declared.
entries.regulatory_note: Defined at 21 CFR 101.60(c)(2). Among other requirements: no sugar or sugar-substituting ingredient may be added during processing; the product may not contain an ingredient containing added sugars such as jam or concentrated fruit juice used to sweeten; the food it resembles normally contains added sugars; and the label must direct consumers to the nutrition panel and state that the food is not low-calorie unless it meets that claim.

entries.name: Sugar free
entries.what: A nutrient content claim meaning less than 0.5 g of sugars per reference amount and per labeled serving, with additional conditions. It does not always mean the product is low-calorie, especially if sugar alcohols or other carbohydrates are present.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses high-intensity sweeteners and/or polyols to hit the sugars line of less than 0.5 g, and then has to follow the claim rules, including a calorie statement in many cases.
entries.regulatory_note: Defined at 21 CFR 101.60(c)(1). The food must contain less than 0.5 g sugars per RACC and labeled serving, must generally contain no sugar ingredient (or use a required 'adds a trivial amount of sugar' statement), and must be labeled 'low calorie' or 'reduced calorie,' or bear a statement such as 'not a reduced calorie food.'

entries.name: Reduced fat
entries.what: A family of nutrient content claims with specific percentage or gram tests, not a casual description. 'Fat free,' 'low fat,' and 'reduced fat' mean different things. A 'reduced fat' product must also be compared to an appropriate reference food.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant takes fat out and often puts water, gums, starches, or proteins back in so the product still has body. Some 'reduced fat' products no longer meet a standard of identity (for example, reduced-fat peanut butter is a 'spread').
entries.regulatory_note: Fat claims are defined at 21 CFR 101.62. 'Fat free' is less than 0.5 g fat per RACC; 'low fat' is 3 g or less; 'reduced fat' is at least 25% less fat than an appropriate reference food, with required comparison language. 'Light' has its own rules in 21 CFR 101.56.

fmg_reveals.title: Reduced Fat Jif isn't peanut butter
fmg_reveals.finding: Reduced Fat Jif isn't peanut butter. Look at the jar, it says Peanut Butter Spread, 60% Peanuts, because FDA requires anything called peanut butter to be at least 90% peanuts.

entries.name: Fat free
entries.what: A nutrient content claim meaning less than 0.5 g of fat per reference amount and labeled serving. Rounding rules can make a very small amount of fat declare as zero.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant that wants this claim often removes fat and then uses gums, starches, sugars, or proteins to rebuild texture — which is why a 'fat free' dairy product can look very different from the full-fat version on the ingredient list.
entries.regulatory_note: Defined at 21 CFR 101.62(b)(1): less than 0.5 g of fat per RACC and per labeled serving, with additional conditions including no added fat ingredient unless a required disclaimer is used.

fmg_reveals.title: Taco Bell's nacho cheese sauce has no cheese in it
fmg_reveals.finding: Taco Bell's nacho cheese sauce has no cheese in it. The list starts with nonfat milk and cheese whey.

fmg_reveals.title: Land O Lakes Fat Free Half & Half is mostly skim milk and corn syrup
fmg_reveals.finding: Land O Lakes Fat Free Half & Half is mostly skim milk and corn syrup. The carton lists skim milk, corn syrup and cream, then 0.5% or less of carrageenan, sodium citrate, dipotassium phosphate, mono and diglycerides, vitamin A palmitate and color added.

entries.name: Made with real…
entries.what: A qualitative claim that the product includes some amount of a named food. It does not, by itself, say how much, and it does not stop the product from being mostly something else.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can use a small amount of the real ingredient — sometimes under 2% — for the claim, while the body of the product is a cheaper substitute, a flavor, or a starch.
entries.regulatory_note: There is no single 'made with real' standard. Claims must not be false or misleading under the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 343). Characterizing-ingredient and flavor-labeling rules in 21 CFR 101.22 apply when the label suggests a food is present as a flavor or as an ingredient.

entries.name: Flavored vs flavor
entries.what: A labeling distinction that matters on the front of the pack. A product can be 'peach flavored' or 'cinnamon flavored' without containing peach or cinnamon. If the characterizing flavor does not come from the food named, FDA rules require wording such as 'flavored,' 'natural flavor,' or 'artificial flavor' so the label is not misleading.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can put a fruit or a spice on the front, use a flavor in the formula, and never put that food on the ingredient list.
entries.regulatory_note: 21 CFR 101.22(i) sets out how a characterizing flavor must be declared, including when the flavor is from the named food, from a natural source other than the named food, or artificial, and when the food itself is not in the product.

fmg_reveals.title: Flavored coffee is sprayed with flavoring after roasting
fmg_reveals.finding: Flavored coffee is sprayed with flavoring after roasting. The solvent that carries the flavor is not listed on the ingredient statement.

fmg_reveals.title: Hot Tamales have no cinnamon in them
fmg_reveals.finding: Hot Tamales have no cinnamon in them. The box says cinnamon flavored, and the heat is artificial flavor.

fmg_reveals.title: Snapple Peach Tea has no peach on the ingredient list
fmg_reveals.finding: Snapple Peach Tea has no peach on the ingredient list. It reads filtered water, sugar, citric acid, tea and natural flavors, with the tea listed after the citric acid.

fmg_reveals.title: Cap'N Crunch Berries have no berries in them
fmg_reveals.finding: Cap'N Crunch Berries have no berries in them. The ingredient list is corn flour, sugar, oat flour, palm or coconut oil, salt and molasses, then Red 40, Yellow 5, Blue 1, Yellow 6 and natural and artificial flavor.

fmg_reveals.title: There is no maple in Mrs. Butterworth's
fmg_reveals.finding: There is no maple in Mrs. Butterworth's. The ingredient list is high fructose corn syrup, corn syrup, water, and under 2% of cellulose gum, salt, molasses, natural and artificial flavor, caramel color, and preservatives.

entries.name: Product of USA
entries.what: For meat, poultry, and egg products regulated by USDA FSIS, a voluntary 'Product of USA' or 'Made in the USA' claim now means the animal was born, raised, slaughtered, and processed in the United States. Multi-ingredient FSIS products have additional domestic-ingredient rules. This is tighter than the older FSIS practice, which allowed the claim on some product that was only processed in the US.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses the claim when the supply chain can support it. Shoppers treated the older, looser claim as origin information it did not always provide.
entries.regulatory_note: FSIS amended its voluntary U.S.-origin claim rules (9 CFR 412.3). For the claim on a single-ingredient product, the animal must be born, raised, slaughtered, and processed in the United States. Multi-ingredient FSIS products must also use domestic ingredients (except spices and flavorings) and be prepared in the United States. See FSIS's final rule on voluntary U.S.-origin claims.

fmg_reveals.title: Beef labeled Product of USA now has to come from cattle born here
fmg_reveals.finding: Since January 1, beef labeled Product of USA has to come from cattle born in the US; before that, imported meat processed at a US plant could carry the claim.

entries.name: Grass-fed
entries.what: A voluntary animal-raising claim on meat. FSIS treats 'grass-fed' and '100% grass-fed' as meaning the animal was fed only forage after weaning (no grain finishing) and was not confined to a feedlot. The claim requires substantiation and prior FSIS label approval.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant or a packer uses it when the cattle program can be documented. It is not the same as 'organic,' and organic certification does not automatically substantiate a grass-fed claim.
entries.regulatory_note: FSIS Guideline FSIS-GD-2024-0006 describes how grass-fed and other animal-raising claims must be substantiated. Unless further qualified, diet claims require that the diet was fed for the lifetime of the animal after weaning.

entries.name: Pasture-raised
entries.what: A voluntary animal-raising claim. For FSIS-regulated meat and poultry, it requires substantiation and prior label approval; the company has to document what 'pasture-raised' means in that system. It is not a single USDA consumer-grade stamp in the way 'USDA Organic' is.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it as a raising-system signal. Without a third-party standard named on the label, the details can vary, which is why FSIS asks for documentation and encourages third-party certification.
entries.regulatory_note: Covered as an animal-raising claim in FSIS-GD-2024-0006. Documentation of controls, traceability, and the meaning of the claim is expected. Third-party certification is encouraged.

entries.name: Cage-free
entries.what: A voluntary raising claim, most often on eggs, meaning hens were not kept in cages and could move around in an indoor house (and, depending on the standard, had access to perches and nest boxes). It does not by itself mean the hens went outside.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A packer uses it to distinguish from caged production. 'Free range' is a different claim and generally implies outdoor access.
entries.regulatory_note: For shell eggs, USDA AMS grading and labeling guidance addresses cage-free claims when USDA is involved; third-party standards also exist. For FSIS-regulated products that bear a cage-free type claim, FSIS-GD-2024-0006 on animal-raising claims applies. There is no single FDA 'cage-free' definition for all foods.

entries.name: Free range
entries.what: A voluntary raising claim. For poultry under FSIS, it generally means the birds had outdoor access, with documentation required. It is not the same as 'pasture-raised' or 'organic,' and the quality of that outdoor access can vary.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it as an outdoor-access signal. Shoppers often hear more in the phrase than the minimum documentation requires, which is why FSIS asks for substantiation.
entries.regulatory_note: FSIS-GD-2024-0006 lists free-range among animal-raising claims that need prior approval and supporting documentation. USDA AMS also addresses free-range in some poultry and egg contexts.

entries.name: Non-GMO
entries.what: Two different systems often get mixed together. USDA's National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard requires disclosure of certain 'bioengineered' foods. 'Non-GMO' is a voluntary marketing claim, often certified by a third party, and is not by itself an FDA definition.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses 'non-GMO' as a shopper signal, especially on products where a common ingredient (corn, soy, canola, sugar beet) is often bioengineered in the US commodity market. The mandatory USDA disclosure, when it applies, is a separate requirement.
entries.regulatory_note: The National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard is administered by USDA AMS (7 CFR Part 66). FDA does not have a separate comprehensive 'GMO-free' definition. Voluntary 'non-GMO' claims still must not be false or misleading.

entries.name: Gluten-free
entries.what: A legally defined claim. In general, the food must not contain gluten-containing grains or ingredients derived from them that have not had gluten removed, and any unavoidable gluten must be below 20 ppm.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it when the formula and the facility controls can meet the 20 ppm standard, which matters for people with celiac disease. 'Wheat-free' is not automatically gluten-free, and 'made in a facility that also processes wheat' is a voluntary advisory, not a substitute for the claim.
entries.regulatory_note: Defined at 21 CFR 101.91. 'No gluten,' 'free of gluten,' and 'without gluten' are held to the same standard. Fermented and hydrolyzed foods have additional recordkeeping rules because testing is more difficult.

entries.name: Keto
entries.what: A marketing claim, not an FDA-defined nutrient content claim. There is no federal standard for how many grams of carbohydrate make a food 'keto.' 'Low carbohydrate' is also not a defined FDA claim in the way 'low fat' is.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses high-intensity sweeteners, polyols, fibers, and fats to hit a shopper's carb target, and then uses 'keto' as a front-of-pack signal. The Nutrition Facts panel is still the enforceable numbers.
entries.regulatory_note: FDA has not established a definition for 'keto' or 'low carb' as a nutrient content claim in 21 CFR Part 101, Subpart D. Claims still must not be false or misleading. 'Sugar free' and fiber declarations, when used, must follow their own rules.

entries.name: Plant-based
entries.what: A marketing term, not a single FDA or USDA standard of identity. It usually means the product is made from plants rather than meat, dairy, or eggs, but the details (how much plant, whether any animal ingredient is present) can vary.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it to position a product against meat or dairy. Standards of identity and 'milk,' 'burger,' and 'sausage' naming have been the subject of FDA and FSIS attention and state laws; the ingredient list still tells you what is in it.
entries.regulatory_note: FDA has issued draft guidance and requests for comment on labeling of plant-based alternatives, but 'plant-based' itself is not a completed standard of identity. Products must not be misleading as to their identity, and allergen rules still apply.

entries.name: Whole grain
entries.what: A grain that still contains the bran, germ, and endosperm in the same relative proportions as the intact grain. '100% whole grain' and 'whole wheat bread' are stronger, more specific claims than 'made with whole grain.'
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses whole-grain flour when it wants the claim and the nutrition profile. It may still blend refined flour in a product that only says 'made with whole grain.'
entries.regulatory_note: FDA's draft guidance on whole-grain label statements describes how the term should be used. Standards of identity for whole wheat bread and similar products are in 21 CFR Part 136. A product labeled only 'wheat bread' is not necessarily whole wheat.

fmg_reveals.title: Ezekiel bread is made without flour
fmg_reveals.finding: Ezekiel bread is made without flour. Food for Life soaks whole wheat, barley, millet, lentils, soybeans and spelt in water until they sprout, then mashes the wet sprouted grain into a dough, adds yeast and salt, and bakes it slow.

fmg_reveals.title: A slice of Dave's Killer Bread has more added sugar than a slice of Wonder Bread
fmg_reveals.finding: A slice of Dave's Killer Bread has more added sugar than a slice of Wonder Bread. On the 21 Whole Grains and Seeds loaf the ingredients go organic whole wheat, water, organic cane sugar, then the grain and seed mix.

fmg_reveals.title: Frosted Mini-Wheats aren't vegetarian
fmg_reveals.finding: Frosted Mini-Wheats aren't vegetarian. The ingredients are whole grain wheat and sugar, then 2% or less of brown rice syrup and gelatin, plus iron and folic acid.

fmg_reveals.title: Nature's Own says no artificial preservatives, but there's a preservative in it
fmg_reveals.finding: Nature's Own says no artificial preservatives, but there's a preservative in it. The 100% Whole Wheat loaf lists it as cultured wheat flour.

entries.name: Multigrain
entries.what: 'Multigrain' means more than one grain was used. It does not mean those grains are whole, and it does not mean the first ingredient is a whole grain. 'Made with whole grain' means some whole grain is present, not that the product is entirely whole grain.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can add a small amount of a second grain, or a little whole-grain flour, and use a front-of-pack phrase that shoppers hear as 'healthier bread' even when the first ingredient is still enriched refined flour.
entries.regulatory_note: There is no FDA standard that makes 'multigrain' equal 'whole grain.' Claims must not be misleading. FDA's whole-grain draft guidance cautions about 'made with whole grain' statements that imply a product is entirely whole grain when it is not.

entries.name: Serving-size tricks
entries.what: Nutrition Facts numbers are declared per serving. By law, serving sizes are based on how much people typically eat (the Reference Amount Customarily Consumed), not on a recommended portion. Rounding rules then allow amounts under certain thresholds to be declared as zero — which is why a cooking spray or a Tic Tac can say 0 calories.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can still follow the rules and get a '0 calorie' or '0g fat' line if the labeled serving is small enough that the actual amount rounds down. Reading the servings-per-container line, and the ingredient list, is how you see the rest of the story.
entries.regulatory_note: Serving size is defined at 21 CFR 101.9(b) and 21 CFR 101.12 (RACCs). Calories less than 5 may be expressed as zero (21 CFR 101.9(c)(1)). Fat and sugars less than 0.5 g may be expressed as zero. These are rounding rules, not a finding that the food contains nothing.

fmg_reveals.title: A Tic Tac is mostly sugar, and the box says 0 calories and 0 carbohydrate
fmg_reveals.finding: A Tic Tac is mostly sugar, and the box says 0 calories and 0 carbohydrate. Sugar is the first ingredient, then maltodextrin, rice starch, gum arabic, flavors, magnesium stearate and carnauba wax.

fmg_reveals.title: A can of PAM olive oil spray says 0 calories and 0 grams of fat
fmg_reveals.finding: A can of PAM olive oil spray says 0 calories and 0 grams of fat. The ingredients are extra virgin olive oil, soy lecithin and dimethyl silicone.

entries.name: % Daily Value
entries.what: A label number that compares the amount of a nutrient in one serving to a reference Daily Value, so you can see whether a serving is high or low in that nutrient. It is not a personal recommendation, and it is not the same as the older '% RDA' wording.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses a high %DV to support a 'excellent source' or 'good source' claim, or a low %DV to support a 'low' claim, when the product meets the claim rules.
entries.regulatory_note: Daily Values and their declaration are set out in 21 CFR 101.9. 'Good source' is generally 10–19% of the DV and 'excellent source' / 'high' is 20% or more, under 21 CFR 101.54, with exceptions.

entries.name: Less than 2% rule
entries.what: An ingredient-list rule, not a nutrition claim. Ingredients present at 2% or less by weight may be listed at the end of the ingredient statement, out of descending-order, if the list uses a quantifying statement such as 'contains 2% or less of …' or 'less than 2% of ….'
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can group a long tail of gums, flavors, colors, preservatives, and 'real' characterizing ingredients at the bottom of the list. That does not mean those ingredients do not matter; it means each one is 2% or less of the formula. A characterizing ingredient in that group may still be the reason for a front-of-pack claim.
entries.regulatory_note: 21 CFR 101.4(a)(2) allows ingredients present in amounts of 2 percent or less by weight to be placed at the end of the ingredient statement following a quantifying statement such as 'Contains __ percent or less of ___' or 'Less than __ percent of ___.'

fmg_reveals.title: A Butterfinger is under 2% cocoa
fmg_reveals.finding: A Butterfinger is under 2% cocoa. The brown coating is palm kernel oil, palm oil and sugar.

fmg_reveals.title: A serving of Campbell's tomato soup has more sugar than a Krispy Kreme glazed donut
fmg_reveals.finding: A serving of Campbell's tomato soup has more sugar than a Krispy Kreme glazed donut. The can lists tomato puree, water, wheat flour and sugar, then under 2% of salt, potassium salt, natural flavoring, citric acid, vitamin C, celery extract and garlic oil.

fmg_reveals.finding: The cheese sauce in Kraft Macaroni & Cheese doesn't list cheese. The blue box packet is whey, milkfat, salt, milk protein concentrate and sodium triphosphate, then under 2% of starch, acids, paprika, turmeric and annatto for color, enzymes and cheese culture.

fmg_reveals.title: Your strawberry Twizzlers have no licorice in them
fmg_reveals.finding: Your strawberry Twizzlers have no licorice in them. The list is corn syrup, wheat flour, sugar and cornstarch, then palm oil, salt, artificial flavor, citric acid, mineral oil, Red 40 and soy lecithin at 2% or less.

fmg_reveals.title: Strawberry Pop-Tarts are 2% or less strawberries

entries.name: Ingredient order
entries.what: Unless an exception applies, ingredients must be listed by common or usual name in descending order of predominance by weight. The first ingredient is the largest; the last is the smallest, except for the 2%-or-less grouping at the end.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Reading the first two or three ingredients is often how you see what the product mostly is — corn syrup before turkey, sugar and palm oil before hazelnuts, water before cream.
entries.regulatory_note: 21 CFR 101.4(a)(1) requires listing by common or usual name in descending order of predominance by weight, with specified exceptions (including the 2% rule and some processing-aid and incidental-additive exemptions in 21 CFR 101.100).

fmg_reveals.title: Snapple Peach Tea has no peach on the ingredient list

fmg_reveals.finding: Athenos is the biggest feta brand in America and it's made from cow's milk. The ingredient list is cultured pasteurized part skim milk, salt, enzymes.

fmg_reveals.finding: Sweet Baby Ray's is corn syrup first.

entries.name: Contains (allergen statement)
entries.what: A required statement for the major food allergens: milk, eggs, fish, Crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, and sesame (added by the FASTER Act). The allergen may be named in the ingredient list in plain language, or in a separate 'Contains' statement, or both.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant has to declare these allergens even when the ingredient name would not otherwise make them obvious (for example, casein, whey, lecithin from soy, flour as wheat). 'May contain' or 'made in a facility' advisories are voluntary and are not a substitute for the required 'Contains' / plain-language declaration of ingredients that are actually in the food.
entries.regulatory_note: Required by the Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer Protection Act and the FASTER Act, codified at 21 U.S.C. 343(w). FDA's allergen guidance explains the 'Contains' format and the nine major allergens, including sesame. 'May contain' statements are not defined in the same statute.

entries.name: Imitation
entries.what: A legal term for a food that is a substitute for and is nutritionally inferior to the food it resembles, or that otherwise must be labeled 'imitation' under FDA rules. 'Imitation vanilla' is a familiar example: it is labeled as imitation because it is not vanilla extract.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses a cheaper substitute and, when the rules require it, has to put 'imitation' on the label. Some substitutes avoid the word by using a different name that does not pretend to be the standardized food (for example, 'cheese product' or 'vanilla flavoring').
entries.regulatory_note: 21 CFR 101.3(e) addresses when a food must be labeled 'imitation.' Vanilla products have standards in 21 CFR Part 169; vanilla extract is 21 CFR 169.175.

fmg_reveals.title: The two bottles of vanilla share one molecule, and you pay for everything else
fmg_reveals.finding: Both pure extract and imitation get their smell from vanillin; a 2 oz pure bottle cost $6.99 and an 8 oz store-brand imitation $1.75 this week, about 16 times as much per ounce for pure.

entries.name: Uncured
entries.what: A meat-label claim that often still involves a cure, just from a vegetable source such as celery powder rather than added sodium nitrite. FSIS requires a qualifying statement such as 'no nitrates or nitrites added except those naturally occurring in …' when that is the case. The product is still a cured-style product in many formulas.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can put 'uncured' or 'no added nitrites' on the front and still get a cured color, a cured flavor, and the antimicrobial effect of nitrite, by using celery or another nitrate-rich ingredient.
entries.regulatory_note: FSIS labeling rules for 'uncured' and 'no nitrates or nitrites added' require a qualifying statement when nitrates or nitrites are supplied by ingredients such as celery powder. See FSIS guidance and 9 CFR labeling requirements for cured products.

fmg_reveals.title: Your uncured bacon is cured
fmg_reveals.finding: Your uncured bacon is cured. Pick up a pack and find the line that says no nitrates or nitrites added except those naturally occurring in celery powder.

entries.name: Non-dairy
entries.what: 'Non-dairy' and 'dairy-free' are not identical. Some older 'non-dairy' creamers still contain a milk protein (caseinate). 'Dairy-free' is generally understood to mean no dairy ingredients, but it is not as tightly defined as an allergen 'Contains' statement. If a milk-derived ingredient is present, milk must still be declared as an allergen.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can position a creamer or a topping against dairy while still using a milk protein for function, unless it is truly free of milk. The ingredient list and the allergen statement are the test.
entries.regulatory_note: FDA has addressed 'non-dairy' products that contain caseinate: if a product contains a milk-derived ingredient, milk allergen declaration is required under 21 U.S.C. 343(w), regardless of a 'non-dairy' claim. A 'non-dairy' claim must not be misleading.

fmg_reveals.title: Coffee-mate costs less to make than half-and-half
fmg_reveals.finding: There is no cream in Coffee-mate. The bottle is water, corn syrup solids and soybean oil.

entries.name: USDA grade
entries.what: A voluntary USDA quality grade, not a safety inspection mark (inspection is mandatory for meat and poultry in commerce). Beef grades (Prime, Choice, Select, and others) are mostly a marbling score. Egg grades (AA, A, B) are quality grades; a carton of USDA-graded eggs can still be several weeks old within the allowed dating rules.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A packer pays for grading because shoppers and restaurants use the shield as a quality signal. It does not tell you how the animal was raised, and it is not a nutrition claim.
entries.regulatory_note: USDA AMS administers official grade standards for beef, eggs, and other commodities. FSIS inspection marks are separate from AMS quality grades.

fmg_reveals.title: A carton of USDA graded eggs can be 7 weeks old on its sell-by date
fmg_reveals.finding: A carton of USDA graded eggs can be 7 weeks old on its sell-by date. Eggs that carry the USDA grade shield have to be eggs of current production when they're packed, which federal rules define as no more than 21 days old.

fmg_reveals.title: The USDA grade on a steak is a marbling score from one slice of the animal
fmg_reveals.finding: The USDA grade on a steak is a marbling score from one slice of the animal. It isn't a safety inspection.

entries.name: Trans fat (0 g claim)
entries.what: A Nutrition Facts rounding statement. If a serving contains less than 0.5 g of trans fat, it may be declared as 0 g. A product can still contain a small amount of trans fat per serving, which adds up if you eat several servings, and the ingredient list may still show a partially hydrogenated oil in older or specialty products.
entries.why_plants_use_it: After PHOs lost GRAS status, most US grocery foods no longer use them, but the '0g trans fat' line is still a rounding rule, not a laboratory zero.
entries.regulatory_note: Under 21 CFR 101.9(c)(2)(ii), trans fat must be declared, and amounts less than 0.5 g per serving may be expressed as zero. FDA's PHO determination separately removed the main industrial source of added trans fat from most food uses.

entries.name: Healthy
entries.what: A voluntary implied nutrient content claim with a specific FDA definition (updated in recent years) based on food-group contribution and limits on certain nutrients. It is not a general wellness adjective when it is used as a claim on a food label.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it when the product can meet the current criteria. The definition has been updated to better match current dietary guidance, so older products may have had to be reviewed.
entries.regulatory_note: The 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim is regulated by FDA (21 CFR 101.65 and FDA's updated 'healthy' rule). Criteria include food-group equivalents and nutrient limits. Check the current regulation for the applicable compliance dates.

entries.name: Excellent source
entries.what: Defined nutrient content claims based on % Daily Value per reference amount. 'Good source' is generally 10–19% of the DV; 'high,' 'rich in,' or 'excellent source' is 20% or more, with some exceptions.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant fortifies, or formulates to a fiber or protein target, so it can put one of these phrases on the front of the pack.
entries.regulatory_note: Defined at 21 CFR 101.54.

entries.name: No hormones added
entries.what: A raising claim whose meaning depends on the species. Federal rules already prohibit the use of added hormones in raising hogs and poultry, so FSIS requires a qualifying statement on pork or poultry that says 'no hormones added' (for example, that federal regulations prohibit the use of hormones). For cattle and sheep, the claim has to be substantiated.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant may want the claim as a shopper signal. On chicken or pork, the qualifying statement is what keeps the claim from implying a difference the law does not allow the competitor to have either.
entries.regulatory_note: FSIS labeling rules and FSIS-GD-2024-0006 address 'raised without hormones' and similar claims, including the required qualifier on poultry and pork. Documentation is required where hormone use is otherwise permitted (cattle, sheep).

entries.name: Raised without antibiotics
entries.what: A voluntary animal-raising claim that must be substantiated and, for FSIS-regulated products, approved on the label. It generally means the animals were not given antibiotics, with documentation from birth (or hatch) to slaughter unless the claim is qualified.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses it as a raising-system signal. FSIS encourages third-party certification because the agency cannot routinely verify farm practices on its own.
entries.regulatory_note: Covered as an animal-raising claim in FSIS-GD-2024-0006, including recommended documentation and third-party certification.

entries.name: Enriched flour
entries.what: Wheat flour with specified amounts of thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, folic acid, and iron added back after milling, and often with barley malt or a dough conditioner. 'Bleached' refers to a flour-treatment step, not to enrichment.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant uses enriched flour because the US standards for white bread, pasta, and many other grain products are built around it, and because it bakes more consistently than a variable whole-grain blend.
entries.regulatory_note: Enrichment standards for flour and related products are in 21 CFR Part 137 (and Parts 136 and 139 for bread and pasta). Folic acid is a required part of the enriched cereal-grain package.

entries.name: Glycerin
entries.what: A sweet-tasting, moisture-holding liquid, used as a humectant in bars, icings, and some 'low sugar' products, and as a carrier for flavors and colors.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It keeps a bar or a frosting from drying out and can add a little sweetness and body without being sucrose.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 182.1320.

entries.name: Propylene glycol
entries.what: A humectant and solvent used to carry flavors and colors, and to hold moisture in some baked goods, icings, and processed foods.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It dissolves flavor oils into a water-based formula and helps a product stay moist on the shelf.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1666, with conditions of use including good manufacturing practice limits.

entries.name: Calcium chloride
entries.what: A salt used as a firming agent in canned vegetables and tofu, as a source of calcium in some cheeses, and in some brines and sports drinks.
entries.why_plants_use_it: It helps a pickle, a canned tomato, or a tofu curd stay firm after heat processing, and it can add a mineral taste in a beverage.
entries.regulatory_note: Listed as GRAS at 21 CFR 184.1193.

entries.name: Standard of identity
entries.what: A federal recipe and naming rule for certain foods (among them peanut butter, milk, bread, vanilla extract, cream cheese, chocolate, and many cheeses). If a product does not meet the standard, it generally cannot use that name — which is why 'reduced fat peanut butter' is a spread, and why some tubs are 'cream cheese spread' rather than cream cheese.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant that wants a familiar name has to meet the standard. A plant that wants a cheaper or lower-fat formula often has to use a different name, or qualify the name, which is a tell on the front of the pack.
entries.regulatory_note: FDA standards of identity are in 21 CFR Parts 130–169. FSIS maintains standards for many meat and poultry products. A food sold under a standardized name must meet the standard unless an exception applies.

entries.name: Cassia
entries.what: The bark most US 'cinnamon' actually comes from. Cassia is a different plant than true (Ceylon) cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum). US labels are not required to say which tree the cinnamon came from. Cassia is also the source of most of the coumarin in cinnamon products.
entries.why_plants_use_it: Cassia is cheaper and has a stronger, more familiar 'cinnamon' punch, so it is what a plant almost always uses in a grocery spice jar, a baked good, or a cinnamon candy — unless the label specifically says Ceylon or true cinnamon.
entries.regulatory_note: US labeling rules do not require a label that says only 'cinnamon' to specify the species. Both cassia and Cinnamomum verum may be sold as cinnamon.

fmg_reveals.finding: US labels need not say which tree your cinnamon came from. Almost certainly cassia, a different plant than true cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum).

entries.name: Cultured wheat flour
entries.what: Wheat flour that has been fermented (cultured) so that organic acids are present, then often dried and added to bread. It functions as a mold inhibitor, similar in job to calcium propionate, with a more kitchen-like name.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can put 'no artificial preservatives' on a loaf and still have a preservative in the formula, listed as cultured wheat flour.

fmg_reveals.finding: Nature's Own says no artificial preservatives, but there's a preservative in it. The 100% Whole Wheat loaf lists it as cultured wheat flour.

entries.name: No artificial preservatives
entries.what: A marketing claim that the product does not use ingredients the plant considers 'artificial' preservatives. It is not a guarantee that nothing in the formula is there to slow spoilage. Cultured flours, cultured dextrose, vinegar, rosemary extract, and celery powder can still be doing that job.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant reformulates to a clean-label preservative and then makes the claim. The ingredient list is where you see what is actually inhibiting mold or bacteria.
entries.regulatory_note: FDA does not define 'artificial preservative' as a single claim standard. Chemical preservatives that have a lasting technical effect generally must be declared (21 CFR 101.22 and 101.100). A 'no artificial preservatives' claim still must not be false or misleading.

entries.name: Added sugars
entries.what: A Nutrition Facts line, required on most packaged foods, that counts sugars added during processing plus sugars from concentrates and similar sources — not the same thing as the ingredient list always showing the word 'sugar.' A product can have added sugars on the panel without 'sugar' as a listed ingredient, for example when a grain is broken down into sugars during processing.
entries.why_plants_use_it: A plant can follow the labeling rules and still surprise a shopper who only reads the ingredient list, or only reads the front of the pack. The added-sugars line is the number the claim rules also look at.
entries.regulatory_note: Added sugars are declared under 21 CFR 101.9(c)(6)(iii). The definition includes sugars added during processing and packaging and certain sugars from concentrates and syrups. A food may show added sugars even when the ingredient list has no ingredient named 'sugar.'
